House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Mr. Fielding, for the second reading of Bill (No. 128) to authorize a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned last night, I had just quoted from a speech where the right hon. gentleman spoke of piles and mountains of information he had in the shape of books, pamphlets and reports from commercial people, surveyors and engineers about the projected railway. Now, with all due regard for books written by travellers, traders or engineers out on hunting or exploration trips, who often make the description of a country as a matter of literary essay, I think it would have been better to have the report of a railway engineer on official duty before engaging the country in such an important undertaking. Had we had such a repoTl before, running the risks of the construction of a new transcontinental railway from Moncton to Port Rupert, through the wild regions of North America, the Rockies and the Laurentian mountains, if we had been patient enough to wait for a report made by serious engineers, I think the mistakes in calculation we know now would have been avoided. We would have been brought nearer to reality, even taking into account the higher grade of the proposed line of railway, the augmented price of materials and labour, together with the constructor's appetite. Again, if there had been competent engineers, the Quebec bridge would not be now lying at the bottom of the St. Lawrence. For my part, I think the construction of the first transcontinental railway was by far more necessary than that of the second one. It was one of the conditions of the entering of British Columbia into

confederation. The west had to be opened to settlement; there was no time to be lost, and each hour delay involved a double loss, as was shown by the event.
This work had been completed for years. Since 1870, the different governments had often attempted to give the contract. The first contract was even entered into, but it was not carried on. So that the plan was laid out, matured and even antiquated. In 1880, when it was proposed to complete the contract and to hand over the railway to the company which had constructed it, my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who was the first lientenant of the leader of the opposition, and every oppositionist member at that time stated that the government was in too great a hurry, that information was needed and that moreover there was no lack of communications with the west. Among others, the right hon, the First Minister, said in an ironical and satirical tone :
The government say-it was the government led by Sir John Macdonald-' accept the contract it is the best we could get.' Is that the language of a free government, of the executive power of a free country ? What has seized the government of this country that they have been compelled to accept this contract from the syndicate? Who in the world compelled the government to negotiate with the syndicate? What great calamity has befallen this country that the government should be compelled to surrender unconditionally to the syndicate? If there had been a war and we had been defeated and the government forced to accept from the victor such terms as suited him to enforce, and if the government came here to have the treaty ratified, would their language have been different to that used in order to induce their supporters to accept the contract? When in the year 1871, at the termination of the disastrous war with Prussia, the provisional government of France met the newly elected national assembly and presented to it the treaty concluded with Germany by which France ceded to that country two of its best provinces, some of the members protested against the clauses of that treaty. And what was the language of the French government in reply? It was exactly the same as used to-day by our administration,:	' Accept the terms, they are the best
we could get.'
In 1884, the company having spent large sums, having exhausted their resources, and having shown by a detailed statement, sworn to by reliable auditors of the expenses incurred to date, and of the -money required to complete the work, and being ai.xious to carry on their contract, which was nearing completion, before the delay elapsed, in spite of the unjust war waged against them by rival companies and jealous capitalists, and offering as a guarantee, not only a section of their Toad, but their whole road, all their holdings without any reservation, to secure a loan of $30,000,000, the government to remit the money only on progress estimates, their proposal was bit-

terly attached by the right hon. the first minister, his leader at that time, the hon. Edward Blake, and their friends. The right hon. gentleman said :
But am I again to repeat what is in the knowledge of everybody, that the Northwest Territories are tapped by the railway system of the continent and that there is communication with it by the lakes, and, therefore, not one more settler would go into that country if the road were opened through its whole length.
And, further:
I would say to the company let your motto We festina lente; take your time but build your road, and it will be for your advantage and the advantage of the people as well.
At that time no one praised the western plains as they are now praised; no one had found out that the west was the granary of Europe and of the whole world. However, that granary had been discovered as early as 1870 by the leaders of the Conservative party, Sir John Macdonald, Sir George Etienne Cartier and Sir Charles Tupper. Yesterday, we heard gentlemen on the opposite side of the House extolling that western granary. Great was my surprise when I heard them. It is the reason why I recall those past events which we are prone to forget.
Now, what did happen in 1903? What a change ! What a transformation ! O !
' quantum mutatus ab illo,' would the Latin poet say.
During a session, the plan of a second transcontinental line is laid out and explained to parliament by the First Minister. It must be approved, and that without delay. There is no more thought of those Prussians who imposed terms so severe upon the French in 1871. It was not Hobson's choice; you had to take it. There was no time to be lost, if it were not too late. Trade was seeking another channel. Our country was in the clutches of the Americans. It was necessary to relieve the situation without waiting any longer.
There was a lack of reports from engineers but it did not matter; the writings and pamphlets of tourists and traders would be used instead! Is it, Mr. Speaker, that, we are to be deprived hereafter of the means of communiaction afforded by the great lakes? Then, the Canadian Pacific Railway is built' and fully operated, but all that goes for nothing. There is need of another transcontinental line, and they must have it now. The late Hon. Mr. Blair is shocked and resigns as the Minister of Railways. To him the whole mystery for he believed there was a mystery-was that the Hon. Senator Cox would not wait any longer. That was the most grievous insult on the part of an ex-member of the cabinet 163
to his former leader and colleague. But it was all to no avail. Everything was settled and patched up in less than no time and the deed was executed.
Mr. Blair was right when he said that the railway could cost $139,000,000, but no body would believe him. The leader of the government had stated that it would cost $13,000,000. His Minister of Finance, going him one better, had mentioned the sum of $11,512,325, so as to have the people believe that he had figured it very closely, since he had found these $325 instead of a round sum. The people gave credit to that information and Mr. Blair kept silent. Wan it on account of his outspoken language or on account of his silence that he was roy ally rewarded by his apointment as chairman of the Railway Commission at a salary of $10,000 a year ? Everybody was pleased. In 1904, the people sanctioned an expenditure of $13,000,000; in 1908, they gave the same verdict, but now they are called upon to face an expenditure ranging between $250,000,000 and $280,000,000.
Neither Mr. Blair nor anybody else had the slightest idea that the work would cost $280,000,000, or that in 1909, before haying completed the prairie section, the sister companies would ask the government for $10,000,000, threatening to stop work in case of a refusal.
Some say it is a loan. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what those gentlemen thought of such loans when they were in opposition ? In 1884 when the Canadian Pacific was asking the government for a loan of $30,000,000, in order to complete the railway, the right hon. the first minister expressed his fears that the loan would be converted into a gift and borrowing the language of the Scriptures he said that he would as soon believe that the waters would flow back from the sea to the lakes as that one cent of that money will ever come back from the Pacific Railway exchequer to the Dominion exchequer. And the Hon. Mr. Blake, the leader of the opposition at that time, spoke of the clause stipulating that - if the company did not refund the money, the government would ' ipso facto ' become proprietor of the railway and he added:
We had other companies which did not lose their roads under similar circumstances. We have had the Grand Trunk, to which we made advances on a first lien, a very first lien, a splendid first lien, and where is that lien now? It is away down among the dead men. I believe it is seen in the Public Accounts and in our balances, but it is visible nowhere else. So it might be here. It is impossible not to recognize the lesson and the story of the past, when looking at the present and trying to forecast the future. Should default be made, you are not going to sacrifice the interests of those shareholders. The past tells what the future will be.
That statesman, that distinguished leadei



of the Liberal party is undoubtedly surprised that the Canadian Pacific Company has so well repaid their indebtedness to the Canadian government and that, on the other hand, his language did not cause the Grand Trunk Railway Company to pay off their mortgages.
That sum (of $10,(MO,000 together with what the Grand Trunk Company of Canada owed us before is a heavy burden upon our people, already overloaded, as the right hon. the first minister used to say. And Mr. Speaker, $7,094,000 of that loan of $10, 000,000 will fall into the exchequer of thf Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, our debtor to the extent of $25,600,000, according to the Minister of Railways and Canals.	-
The hon. Minister was asked whether the G. T. P. Company would again ask parliament for other sums of money and the hon. gentleman answered that he could not tell, although it was quite possible.
'As for myself, I am free to see that this request of the company shall be granted though the sureties that are offered are worth nothing, as we have it from the mouth of the hon. Minister of Finance himself in his speech of the 30th of March last. Our guarantee only affects the prairie section which is under construction and only amounts to a fourth mortgage. A second and perhaps a third similar request will soon follow. They shall all be granted and the mortgages-in the terse style of the' hon. Mr. Blake will be away down among the dead men.
How powerful are the railway companies m this country of ours. They are in full control of everything, ' de facto,' if not ' de jure.' The more I look into the matter, the more I am confirmed in my belief, and the speeches delivered in 1884 by the then members of the opposition are of a nature to satisfy me entirely as to the correctness of my assumption. I am unable to resist the temptation of quoting some of their fine oratory. That debate was also in connection with a loan of thirty millions to the Canadian Pacific Railway. What were the grounds for granting that loan ? No other grounds can be shown, stated the right hon. gentleman to-day leader of the government :
That the government are to-day controlled by a power mightier than they. Thev are like the wizard of old, who, through his incantations, gave life to a monster which made him its slave and in the end destroyed him. the governments are in the hands of a company which it must obey, just as the servant in the Scripture, to whom his master said: Go, and he goeth; come, and he cometh.'
Then Sir Richard Cartwright on the same occasion put the following query to the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Ives):
' Does the hon. member suppose that the

Canadian Pacific Railway Company has no paid advocate in this House? Does he suppose that no member is interested in favouring the Canadian Pacific Railway? Does he imagine that the company has no friends in the House and in the cabinet?
Mr. Speaker, when men of the standing of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister and Sir Richard Cartwright, men of exceptional intelligence and wisdom, veterans in parliament, experienced speakers possessing the art of expressing all they wish to convey and of conveying nothing more than what they really wish to say, express themselves in such a manner before the House, it is not surprising that we, the new members of the House, should feel serious misgivings when we see all the Grand Trunk Companies besieging parliament for new favours.
Do not these speeches, Mr. Speaker, in the light of the facts before us concerning the difference of $775,0000 as between the $27,031,453 submitted by the company as chargeable to future construction on the 31st December, 1908, and that of $26,256,455 really approved, in the light of that other item of $162,000, of which so much has been said but no explanation yet given, and which the Grand Trunk Company of Canada holds against the Grand Trunk Pacific Company of Canada-are we not justified, I say, to apply to the Grand Trunk Pacific and to the present government what was said in 1884 of the government of that time.
If at one time the Pacific ruled, to-day the Grand Trunk Pacific commands. The position is the same, only the name has changed. That is the least that can be said. It is a painful, but logical, conclusion which cannot be denied.
When governments make advances to railway companies under such circumstances, they should, it seems to me, insist upon the transfer to the country of an amount equal to such advances in paid up privileged and common stock of the company, and so become to all intents and purposes shareholders of the company until such advances have been refunded in full. That would be a good, practical security, besides giving the government means of controlling the companies. In the present case, the government should require bonds from the company and the latter could not refuse; if the bonds are in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, that company could not refuse. For my part, I consider such security better than any mortgage, to which I attach little importance.
(Translation.) Would the hon. member allow me to put a question? What are the bonds of any company worth if they are not paid up in full?

(Translation.) There would be no risk in accepting such bonds, and for my part I would not hesitate to accept them. They are a much better security than the mortgages of which Mr. Blake spoke, and which are gone the way of last year's snows.
If we had acted in that way towards the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada, is it not probable that we would have recovered the sum of $25,000,000 still due and which, as Hon. Mr. Blake said, is to be found nowhere except in the public accounts? To me the thing appears clear.
You are easily satisfied.

Perhaps I may not require as much as you do. The Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada never paid these mortgages because the net profits of the company never covered its first bonds. And those bonds were never covered on account of enormous promotion costs and lobbying costs and of other expenses of a more or less legitimate nature which the company was obliged to defray at every step, because excessive salaries and perquisites were paid to managers and administrators, to princes of finance, to lawyers and to those friends whom Sir Richard Cartwright mentioned in 1884, and who seem to have been everywhere even within the precincts of parliament and in the cabinet.
History repeats itself ; that is the reason why the privileged bonds and other stock of such a company are better security than mortgages.
The Hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals told us yesterday the country was in partnership with the company for the construction of this railway. If such be the case, Canada must be the sleeping partner providing the funds without any hope of sharing in the profits. But are we in partnership with the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Company of Canada or any other company springing from the original Grand Trunk Company? I mentioned yesterday two of those new creations. It appears that I had forgotten a third, the Grand Trunk Construction Company. We may perhaps be in partnership with them as long as it is necessary to disburse money but when the day of reckoning comes we will find only the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the probable inheritor of all the debts. Town lots, hotels and parks will belong to some other of those companies, branch lines to a third, and still another will crop up at all points with privileged claims for works and construction. The Grand Trunk Pacific will hold all the indebtedness. I would prefer having to deal with one single company, the Grand Trunk 1631
Company of Canada. That company should come forward alone and openly to take charge of the whole construction and incur the full responsibility of the advances now sought for. They should take charge of the whole road, of branch as well as trunk lines, and hold in their own name city lots and all other assets; such a proceeding would be more reassuring for this House and for the government. For my part, Mr. Speaker, if I were in the place of the government of Canada, before granting this loan of ten millions to the Grand Trunk Pacific,
I would require, besides the conditions I have just mentioned, bonds and a settlement of old accounts on the part of the Grand Trunk Company. I would liquidate the old claim. Yes, Mr. Speaker, that is what I would do, and that is, no doubt, what the government will do, unless they have fallen under the influence of that old magician of which the right hon. Premier spoke in 1880 and 1884, whose life, says the story, was constantly threatened by the claws and teeth of the strange progeny he had begot, as it turned out, to his own undoing.
This railway, Mr. Speaker, is a hastily conceived idea of the present administration. One might suppose that it was suggested to the hon. gentlemen now holding power by the magician of the story or by some mischievous imp for the purpose of placing them in contradiction with their past, of giving us a further proof of the weakness of human nature and of showing us how the finest political intellects must of necessity contradict themselves several times in the course of their career, especially when having long remained in the cold shades of the opposition they are at length called upon to bask in the golden rays of power.
The other evening I heard with pleasure the statement made by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Pardee), that the great Canadian statesman, Sir John Macdonald, had been unwisely opposed at the time to the construction of the first- transcontinental. Yes, Mr. Speaker, that patriot was unwisely and injudiciously opposed in a great national undertaking, and the wonder is that he was able to accomplish his task in spite of the opposition he met with. Everyone will admit that the construction of the first transcontinental was a more difficult and especially a more necessary undertaking than the present and that the prosperity we have since enjoyed, and of which our opponents are wont to boast, is is great part due to that railway. Those words of the member for Lambton West are an act of justice, of tardy justice towards the memory of a great man; I thank the hon. member for them and I congratulate him, the more so that it must have

cost him an effort to say that which implied a censure against his leaders.
In spite of my criticisms and certain expressions, perhaps rather harsh, that I have borrowed from opponents for the purposes of debate, I accept, I repeat it, the accomplished fact and I am ready to second all legitimate and advantageous measures calculated to carry the work to a successful termination. But while accepting the situation, let us act like business men and like freemen, not like the vanquished of 1870, of whom the right hon. premier spoke in 1880.
_ First of all, if all these companies are not in a position to build the road, should we not be immediately advised of the true situation. Then, if the government is- obliged to advance all the money, would it not be preferable to pay to the companies the value of the work they have done and take up the road as state property, with a view of disposing of it as soon as possible in favour of the company which may be in the best position to work it and especially to pay for it.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, if to secure the success of that colossal enterprise to which the country is mow bound, it is necessary for us to grant this loan and to become the bankers of the companies, let us at all events stipulate that they will pay interest at a rate at least as high as that which the government itself is obliged to pay. The interest on the loan to the companies is fixed at 4 per cent, but the government may have to pay more than that; why not stipulate, therefore, that the companies shall pay whatever interest the government may be obliged to pay on loans?
Would it not also be advisable to make an attempt tending towards the settlement of the old claim of $25,000,000 due to the country by the Grand Trunk Company of Canada? If the claim must be lost, let us make the sacrifice at once and hear no more about it. If on the contrary, the claim is of any value, should we not attempt to have it paid? When favours are asked conditions may be imposed. The Grand Trunk Company of Canada owes us $25,000,000 and wishes to borrow $10,000,000 more.
Is it not time that we should say to them:	We will give you this money, but
at the same time we shall settle this old claim which dates away bgck before confederation. In one word, let us compel them to give us as security a certain amount of shares in the capital stock of the company, either common or preferred stock; let us become shareholders of the company. It is, according to mej the best security, a far better security than those mortgages in which Mr, Blake no more than I had any confidence whatever.
What are those shares bringing to-day?
I must confess they are bringing very little just now, but before long they will be worth double their present value.
Mortgages will have to be paid first.

No doubt mortgages will have to be paid first, but the stock will always have a market value, and the government can always dispose of them to some advantage, while a mortgage like that which is held by the government against the Grand Trunk Railway is valueless, inasmuch as the government lacks the manliness to compel them to pay.
To conclude, I say that I am bound to accept the fait accompli, and that we must make the best possible arrangements with the company in order to ensure the proper carrying out of this huge project wherein is pledged the good name of the nation.
Mr. ALEXANDER McCALL (Norfolk) Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks on the question before the House, I need scarcely ask that the courtesy always extended to new members will be extended to me. I am glad to observe a spirit of fairness prevailing on both sides. In discussing this question, I cannot hope to touch upon more than a few phases of it, for it is too great a question for me to discuss in its entirety. But representing, as I do, one of the first organized counties in this Dominion, a county whose people have for more than a hundred years contributed to its taxes and to the cost of every public work, I wish to give voice to their sentiments on this question. Being a thrifty people, who have suffered hardships for the good of this nation, who in their early days gave of their strength to the nation's defence and to making the country habitable and fit to enjoy life in, they may justly feel some alarm at a proposition that means doubling their liabilities, and I would be unfaithful to them, if I failed to say something on the question before the House this afternoon.
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals spoke of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway as a partnership. That idea is a good one. In reality, there are three parties to the partnership, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, the administration of the day, and the people of this country. In a business partnership it is a fundamental principle that all parties must be absolutely lair with each other. One must not take advantage of or be untrue to another, or else the partnership fails. Applying this thought to the proposed resolution, I think I can safely say that the people of Canada, the third party in the partnership, have not

been treated fairly by the second party, the government of the day. Is there a gentleman in this House who will say seriously that if the people of this country had believed that they were facing a $300,000,000 proposition, or a $250,000,000 proposition, or even a $200,000,000 proposition, they would have ratified it four years ago? I will not take up the time of this House in discussing the promises made by the ministers as to the cost of the work to the country, whether it was $13,000,000 or $14,000,000, or which it was; but I say that a proposition which simply doubles the liabilities of this country, which increases the net debt of the country from $250,000,000 to $500,000,000, which places our liabilities at half a billion dollars, is not one that will receive the approval of the people of this country when placed before them in that bald, plain way. Therefore, I say that the third party in this partnership, the people of Canada, have been grossly deceived by the second party, the government, in the interest of the first party, the railway company, who did nothing but drive a very hard bargain with the government and now not only hold them to that bargain, but come and ask for this loan of $10,000,000, and the Minister of Railways and Canals would not say that this was the last call that he expected them to make. Instead of that, he rather intimated that there would be another call, and perhaps others after that. Clearly that is a breach of faith towards the third party in this transaction. To me and to others on this side of the House the Minister of Railways and Canals seems to have treated this important question in a spirit of levity. He spoke in a jocular way of the increased cost of the undertaking as a matter of course, referring to the Panama canal, the Erie canal and other canals whose cost outran the estimates of the engineers. But it is to be noted that the Panama canal will one day carry the ships of every nation, whose flags float the seas, and if it is to cost $400,000,000, the cost is to be borne by eighty million people, twelve times our population; and yet the sum to be expended on that one work is not much larger than the sum we are called upon to expend on this scheme. I am not discussing that proposition by way of comparison with this; but the point I wish to make is that if the cost of the work turns out to be anywhere from 50 per cent to 200 per cent more than the estimate of the engineers, then in estimating the cost of a work of this kind, after the engineers have done their worst, so to speak, the government should say to the people of Canada: ' While our engineers have estimated this work to cost $100,000,000, we will be frank with you and will say that it will cost $200,000,000 ; ' you are going to pledge our future earnings and those of our children to this stupendous scheme, and we should know the liability we are to share. Need I ask this House if that information was given to the; people of this country, so that they could vote no to the proposition if they chose? No, the reverse was the case.
Much was said by the Minister of Railways and Canals about the quality of the railway. Well, we ought to get the best railway in the country or on the continent, but I do not believe that the plans and estimates provide for this. Every one who knows anything about railway construction knows that the first consideration is a good tie. If you have a good tie, you can do with an indifferent rail and roadbed. An American standard tie is a tie 8 feet 6 inches long, 7 inches thick, 8 inches wide. The Pennsylvania, one of the great trunk lines in the United States uses a tie of those denominations, made of southern pitch pine or white oak. Bear in mind that that is the standard tie used by all the eastern trunk lines in the United States. But just consider the ties which are being laid on the National Transcontinental Railway-8 feet long, 6 inches thick, and 7 inches wide, and made of the cheapest timber known, namely, jack pine and tamarack. The roadbed and the rail may be sufficient, but that tie is not one which can stand any heavy traffic. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mt. Graham) speaks about the high standard of the road. Well, time will tell whether we get a freight standard road or not. In fact, it is a railway still on paper, and it will require actual observation when completed to see whether the minister's promises are made good or not.
I am not going to discuss the price. The great question is whether we are getting value for it. In dealing with the cost of this Toad, from the standpoint of our national resources, I propose to offer a few words; and I would ask hon. gentlemen to bear with me if I should appear careless and drop a million or two when dealing with the millions of this country. In handling hundreds of millions, one might easily drop an odd million or so, but our liabilities will not fail to turn up in good order. They will all be in their place when the time for payment comes and will have to be met by the tax payers. Before this country began to pay out money on account of the Transcontinental, our public debt was about $258,000,000. This sum represents all the debt of all the provinces at their entry into the confederation and all of the debts of the Dominion to the time of the announcement of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Taking the most moderate estimate-and I have not heard the Minister of Railways attempt this session to say just what sum of money is necessary to complete the work-this entire road, the eastern section, the prairie and the mountain sections and the government guarantee, will require $250,000,000.

That is a moderate estimate of our liabilities which must be paid within the next four or five years, making $500,000,000 in all. Admitting that to be the case, ought we not alh to feel anxious that the country should keep its expenditures within its capacity to bear the burden? But that expenditure is not all we are committed to. There are other schemes which are bound to become national liabilities. For instance, the Hudson Bay Railway and the Georgian Bay canal. In connection with the latter scheme, the right hon. the Prime Minister last year said it was one which was near to his heart; and when the right hon. gentleman says that a scheme is near his heart and puts his hand there, that is good for a million. I hope we shall not have too many such schemes.
It is true that some people from a county right near the city of Toronto, came oveT here and asked for a sum of about a million, and it is said that there were a number of Tories in that delegation and that through their influence a sum was granted for the proposed expenditure. Let me say to the Prime Minister that if he knew the Tories of North York as some of us do, he would not give them a quarter of a million. He must not be too credulous on such occasions because when Tories come in company with Liberals, it is a sure sign that they are after the public treasury.
As I have said, other expenditures will be necessary, and we ought not to tie ourselves up to one large outlay, but must leave something to meet other requirements. Great questions are coming up and great obligations which will need money, and in this one matter of the National Transcontinental scheme, we have been altogether too generous. This scheme ought not to have been brought up at the time it was. We should have waited until the public demand was more insistent, and then, in estimating the cost of the road, we should have figures to submit to the country, based on the full knowledge of the extent of the burden we were assuming.
The question comes right here :	What
are you going to do about it ? That is the question we are facing to-day. Not only have we to meet the original obligation, but we are asked to pay another $10,000,000. Is there any guarantee that we may not be asked for still another $10,000,000 and still another until the entire cost of this transcontinental railway will be on the debt side of the ledger. You will find that the whole cost of the road will be our investment, and that in return we will assume 100 per cent of the risk and have none of the profits, whereas the Grand Trunk Railway will get all the profits, if there be any, and not have invested a cent in the undertaking. Would it not be pos-Mr. McCALL.
sible at this stage to reconsider this scheme? Would it not be possible to ask for an extension of the time of the New Brunswick section? It is patent to every one that the New Brunswick section must compete with our own Intercolonial Railway and thereby render that railway of less value. Why should not the construction of the eastern portion of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton be delayed? The western section and the outlet to Lake Superior could be pushed rapidly so as to give that country an outlet to the lake. The traffic of that country is largely during the season of navigation. This might not only enable them to finance this scheme but it would look better to the country, and the feeling of the people that they have been deceived would gradually disappear. There is no question, this proposed loan will be made ; whether it meet with the approval of members on this side or not, it will be voted. I am glad to hear the expressions from hon. members on this side that they assume responsibility for this work and declare that it must eventually be pushed through to completion. I admit that I share in the belief expressed by hon. gentlemen opposite that that western country is a country of great promise, one that will need further outlets than those already provided.
I urge again upon the government due consideration for those who have really made the wealth of this country. We are the sons of the pioneers who came here in the latter-part of the seventeenth century and in the early part of the eighteenth century, and, not only bore the burden of the defence of this country, but built it up, establishing and maintaining law and order, living thrifty lives and laying the foundations of our national wealth. The savings of our people in the government savings banks and in the chartered banks of our country help to finance these great schemes that we discuss in this parliament. There were periods in the lives of these pioneers when the failure of a harvest or the coming of illness into the home made their lives a tragedy. They faced destitution and want at times. Some regard should be paid to the sentiments of people of that class. If we succeed, it will be upon their thrift and energy. In a question of this kind, involving such a large sum of money, a scheme that means the doubling of our national obligations ought not to be entered upon. The people ought to be treated at all times by the ministers who have charge of the public expenditure in a serious spirit, and in an earnest way, so that their expressions may command respect among the people. I hope that parliament will consider this question, perhaps I should say more ser-

iously than it has, but in the light of our ability to bear the enormous burden of this Grand Trunk Pacific scheme. Whatever may be the result, even should our worst fears be realized, we can depend upon the Canadian people to meet the responsibility with the high courage characteristic of the nation to which we belong.

1 do not wish to unnecessarily delay the House in going into committee on the proposed Bill, but I do desire to make a few general observations before the matter is specifically dealt with by way of amendment in committee. And I may add that my justification for so doing must be the fact that I have gone through two long and wearisome campaigns with the Grand Trunk Pacific matter, affording a great deal of ammunition in those campaigns. I followed very carefully the different speeches made in this Grand Trunk Pacific debate since the Finance Minister introduced the resolution. While concurring, as members of both sides of the House do, that it is desirable that this work should finish speedily and efficiently, I wish to utter my protest against the methods adopted and the statements made by the government, and also against the extraordinarily favourable position in which this company has been placed in contradistinction to the position occupied by the people of Canada. I notice that the general line of argument adopted by the government has been designed to show that we, as members of the Conservative party, are opposed to the construction of this road. Probably the wish is father to the thought when these arguments are adduced. Secondly, they attempt to say that they are doing what we did as a Conservative party in connection with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. And, thirdly, we have been treated to a great many elaborate and very misleading statements indeed as to the supposed wholesale and sweeping endoTsation of the government's policy by the people. Let me refer for half a moment to the first line of argument that the supporters of the government have been taking during this whole debate. Coupled with and reinforcing the argument that we are opposed to the construction of the road have been some magniloquent speeches as to the greatness of this country, given to the House 1 ore rotundo ' and implying how small is the faith of members on this side in the country in which our lot is cast. It is a rather singular attitude for the Liberal party to take. I have no desire to dwell upon this point, because these pyrotechnic utterances are not intended to deceive anybody. I suppose we all have our party balloons to inflate, and duly inflate them. But I would point out that it is comparatively easy to
display faith when somebody else has blazed the way and, by noble foresight and high endeavour, has laid the foundations on which we of the later generation can happily and safely build. Hon. members on the other side need not distress themselves as to the faith in our country of a party whose leader, in the teeth of most appalling difficulties, consummated the policy of opening up the vast hinterland which was literally terra incognita in those days, and made it possible for the people of my own province of British Columbia to unite their fortunes with those of the people of Eastern Canada. The The name of Sir John Macdonald will ever stand out as that of a man having faith and faith accompanied with great works. The party which took so large a part in laying deep and broad the foundation of this nation which has coupled the east and the west, which established a trade policy which has now lasted for thirty years, will not be found lacking at this particular time in the most whole-hearted efforts in advancing the interests of the country and heightening its prosperity. But in doing so it by no means follows that we have to endorse every phase and every detail of the great scheme now under consideration, and which in so many of its details and phases is so regardless and careless of the rights and true interests of the oeople of Canada.
The second line of argument addressed to the House by hon. gentlemen opposite was a comparison with the Canadian Pacific Railwav. I do not wish to deal at length with that. I would say, however, that the comparison is a most unfortunate one for those who make it. It has been pointed out in this House that the Liberal party themselves, between 1873 and 1878, made as large or larger offers of land grants and money to the Canadian Pacific than the Conservative party made. The attitude of our friends opposite is somewhat changed in recent years. I notice that last session the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) so far from taking the attitude which our friends the enemy delighted to take in years gone by, stated that we had liberally assisted and aided the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that it was not for him to sav, and he would not say, that we had aided and assisted them too liberally. Then I need only point out also that in regard to this loan the difference is so vital and so marked that it is remarkable that the argument is used at all, and the comparison made. In that admirable speech that was delivered by my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) on this subject some time ago, he showed the fundamental difference that existed between this loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific and the loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway some years ago, of $30,000,000. He pointed

out that the Canadian Pacific Kailway people pledged their land, their railway, their equipment, their branch lines, the whole institution, lock, stock and barrel, and repaid the whole thing within two years. For that reason, I say, it is astonishing that a comparison of this kind is made by our friends opposite, and one cannot but think that if it is made, it cannot be made in good faith.
Now this loan only accentuates the free and easy way in which the government has been dealing with this House on behalf of a company which was in a sense a partner of the government. I listened attentively yesterday to the speech of the Minister of Railways and Canals. We on our side of the House, I think many of us, always listen with a good deal of pleasure to that bon. gentleman. He is so good natured that he compels a certain amount of acceptance, although we have to dissent from a good many of his arguments. I must say that his speech yesterday certainly stamps him as the Harold Skimpole of the government side. He has the same dazzling way of dealing with figures, he also has that magnificent disregard of responsibility that characterized the gentleman I have referred to. Like Harold Skimpole, I think the Minister exhibits also the same easy disdain of such gross and material things as days of reckoning, and discharge of liability. The Minister of Railways yesterday laboured the idea of partnership. I think his words were that he did not believe that we should get stock for the accommodation we were giving the company, that it was rather a sordid idea, and that we must finance this railway because we have to carry it through at all costs, because we were in partnership. That is true, but after all the Canadian people, one party in partnership will be called upon in future time to pay very high rates on the enormous cost of construction to a company which had apparently never assumed any serious obligations, and who will reap all the profits. Last session the attitude of the Minister of Railways was slightly different. He figured it out on that occasion that the total liabilitv, that is the actual cash we should have to pay would be $38,263,976 for the benefits we receive from this through line from Moncton to the Pacific coast. He added that if:
Instead of taking this out of revenue we borrowed it at 3 per cent,-I find that for the great benefit we will receive this country will have to pay annually the sum of $1,1*4,-[DOT]'19.28.
Before finishing his speech he also added:
I believe the Grand Trunk Pacific Company will never call on the Dominion of Canada to pay one cent of the guarantee of the bonds, nor one cent of the 3 per cent interest on the cost of the railway.

The fact that instead of borrowing at 3 per cent, we have had, as my hon. friend from St. Antoine pointed out the other day, to pay something like 4i per cent, for the last big loan, and something like $450,000 in commission, besides brokerage charges, and the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific are now coming to us for another loan of $10,000,000, I presume, won't disturb the Minister of Railways at all as he apparently regards this whole thing in an extremely light and jovial spirit. He introduced a new line of argument yesterday, he had to face facts to some extent, and he attempted to draw a parallel with other great lines of railways and with undertakings in other countries. For instance ha tried to draw a parallel between it and the Erie canal, an unfortunate illustration, as that undertaking was permeated through and through with the most gigantic graft. Then he dealt with the Panama canal. He seems rather prone to draw his illustrations from canals. The other day he defended the Newmarket canal, and now he is treating us to arguments which remind us, not only of Harold Skimpole's methods, but of Mark Twain's humour, so that it is hard for us to take him seriously. The Minister of Railways also stated as a justification for this loan, that the matter had been discussed on the hustings in 1904 and 1908, this question had been discussed in all its bearings, the voice of the people had been asked, and they had given it ample endor-sation.
Now, I would like to consider that argument for a moment. In 1903 we had a speech from the Throne, which, as speeches from the Throne are usually supposed to do, should have outlined broadly the policy of the government for that session. There was no allusion made to this project at all. There was, as I remember, only a reference to the fact that the needs of transportation were considerable, and a commission was to be appointed to go into that question. But nothing was done, or little was done. But to the astonishment, not only of the House but of the country, the right hon. gentleman who leads the fortunes of the Liberal party, about five months after the House met, divulged a plan which embraced, to all intents and purposes, the present Grand Trunk Pacific Railway scheme from ocean to ocean. Now in spite of the right hon. gentleman having shelved that commission, in spite of any defence he might have offered for that scheme, yet he was entitled to credit for originating a great idea and disclosing the scheme, although it was only a scheme in embryo. But if he had later on submitted it in skeleton to the House and country to see with what sympathy it would be received, noword of criticism could have been offered*

if it had been endorsed by the people of the country no one would have said anything deprecating the project. But what actually happened? Nothing of the sort. Without any mandate from the people at all for a scheme of so gigantic a character, we find the right hon. gentleman was closeted with one of the most astute railway magnates on this continent, for a long time, and that, desirous of the kudos which should perhaps rightly attach to the formation of any large scheme, he allowed himself to be outwitted in every part of the game, and we had the scheme forced through parliament, the government refusing to wait either for advice or for the people's opinion. One of the ministers, Mr. Blair, said that he urged him to wait, and that if he didn't wait it must be because there was an absence of any really good and substantial argument to sustain the case. We know that Mr. Blair, the only gentleman who was thoroughly conversant with railway affairs in the government at that time, was villified on that side of the House. Later on he was promoted or rewarded by ai very high post, because the government usually find that it is the better way of silencing opponents. Now when that agreement was finally signed, sealed and delivered, and supposed to be lived up to, hon. gentlemen will remember what happened. Sir Charles Rivers Wilson, president of the railway company, in speaking to his shareholders after the close of that session, told them that he had succeeded in driving the government into adopting a position more favourable to the company, that is, in amending the contract. I do not think there is any doubt that from that day to this the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific have insistently and persistently driven the government of this country. The government called another session of parliament for the purpose of considering the ratification of the altered or amended contract. We all know the great differences between the original and the amended contract. I am not going into that matter in detail except to point out one or two of these differences. We contended that the original contract was unfair to the people of Canada, but we were assured by the government that it was a fair contract and that at all events it was finally settled. Yet, we find, amongst a great many other serious alterations, alterations of a vital character that, whereas, before the people had undertaken to guarantee three-quarters of the bonds of the mountain section of this road up to a limit of $30,000 a mile, afterwards that was amended by striking out the words '$30,000 a mile', and we undertake now to guarantee three-quarters of the cost of the mountain section to an unlimited amount. At
the commencement of the session in which this change was made the mover of the address stated that while this was an important amendment the road might cost $30,000 a mile or it might cost less. When the prairie section is costing about $35,000 a mile it is a bold man who would estimate the cost of the mountain section, although I understand that the government, or the railway company, have put it somewhere about $80,000 per mile. Then, in paragraphs 31, 32 and 33 of the old contract there was at least some provision made for securing the people if the company fell down. There was some right of foreclosure. If the government felt called upon to pay the interest on the bonds after a specified time there was some little security offered. We find in the amended contract that it is amended in such a way that practically all the security is done away with. In paragraph 6 we find these words:
Notwithstanding anything in the said contract contained, the government shall not exercise any rights in respect of possession, foreclosure or sale, by reason of non-payment of interest by the company under the thirty-first, thirty-second or thirty-third paragraphs of the said contract, or under all or any of them, unless and until there shall be such default to the extent in the whole of a sum equal to five years of such interest, as the company is not relieved from payment of or permitted to defer or capitalize by the provisions of the said paragraphs.
We find that the limited right that we had in the shape of a foreclosure, the little security we had in the first contract, was so interfered with by the amended contract that every safeguard is done away with and is reduced to so shadowy a point that it is impossible to see anything except that if the undertaking should prove unprofitable the government are at liberty to take it over and then they may hand it back when the affairs of the company have become more prosperous. There are other important differences which I shall not touch upon. It was not enough that this amended contract was bad but, by the aid of the government supporters, it was put through parliament immediately before an appeal to the country was made. That may have been a good party move, I do not say it was not, but to say that the result was the voice of the country in even a partial way is to say something which is absolutely untrue. When our friends say that they have been sustained and that they have the confidence of the people, I would like to ask them what sort of an endorsation it was. They had the people tied hand and foot to a contract of this sort before the appeal was made. What was the character of the whole campaign?

We were told throughout the length and breadth of this country the one horrible thing that was presented to the people by Conservatives was the repudiation of a contract solemnly entered into by the government. That word 'repudiation' would have such an ugly sound that no true Canadian would dream of supporting a man who would put forth a policy of that kind. The people were told that every Conservative candidate was opposed to the construction of the road, and that if the Conservative party were put in control the scheme would be destroyed. This repudiation phrase was worked to a finish throughout my own province and not only that but gentlemen supporting the Liberal government in British Columbia laid enormous stress upon the question of speedy construction. My hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) who, I am sorry to see, is not in his place, particularly made great efforts in that direction. He assured the people of the Pacific coast, that, although there was nothing in the contract to that effect, he had Mr. Hay's assurance that the road would be commenced at once. They so persuaded the people of British Columbia that construction was going on at once that, in their desire for the early construction of the road, and in their natural deprecation of anything that savoured of repudiation, it is perhaps small wonder that the whole of that province went Liberal at that time. If, however, they had known what the facts were, if they had known that not a sod was to be turned in British Columbia for four years it is natural to assume that we would have seen a different state of things. There is an old saying that once bitten twice shy. The same appeal was made last fall, the same arguments were advanced, but, although British Columbia wanted to see that road built and although the people there still have faith not only in the road but in the country, the result was that while there was a Liberal majority in 1904 of 2,872, there was a Conservative majority of 4,091 in 1908. In the first contract which was put before the people of the country we were assured, as the right hon. gentleman who formulated the scheme also assured us, that there was a tremendous haste for the thing to go through. There was a clause which dealt with the time and which placed the completion of the road in the year 1908. In paragraph 10 of the contract we have this:
The work of locating and constructing the said western division shall be commenced forthwith after the ratification of this agreement by the parliament of Canada, and shall proceed with the utmost dispatch and shall be completed within five years from the first Mr. BURRELL.
day of December, 1903, unless prevented by the act of God, the King's enemies, internal disturbances, epidemics, floods or other causes beyond the control of the company.
This, as we know, was altered in this amended contract to 1911 and the word 'strikes' was also put in after these other contingencies which were mentioned.	I
might point out that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) made a good deal of the unforeseen and tremendous difficulties that they had met with and what had resulted in bringing about the present position of affairs. I do not know that the King's enemies, or any act of God, or floods or strikes, have greatly interfered with the operations of the company. 1 might illustrate that point by a very short allusion. Some time ago a case was brought up by a certain farmer against a man to whom he had leased his land. One of the stipulations of the lease was that the land was to be left in as good a state as when the tenant had taken it, as to the seeding down to wheat and so on, unless the act of God interfered. It seems that the tenant did not leave it in as good a state, and when the case came up for trial one of the points to be decided was whether the act of God had anything to do with it or whether it was due to the man's own fault, and the jury brought in a verdict that there had been damage and that the fault was partly that of the defendant and partly God's. I take it that the present government, who are so ready to ignore the existence of a kind providence when things are going smoothly, will always contend, when things are not going smoothly, that it, is the act of God. The haste which was so necessary in 1903 and which led the government to allow the company only until 1908 to finish their construction was forgotten, and the time extended to January, 1911. I do not think that any sane man believes that 1911 will see anything like the completion of the road. The government brag that they have been endorsed by the people, but that endorsation is of no value under the circumstances. In the olden times, when the country was supposed to be afflicted with witches, a test, known to every one acquainted with history, was employed to determine whethex a woman was a witch or not. The woman suspected had her right thumb tied to her left big toe and her left thumD tied to her right big toe, and, thus bound, she was thrown into a pond. If she sank she was not a witch and was unfortunately drowned. If she did not sink she was a witch and was unfortunately burned. That is like the test that was applied to public opinion in this case. The government tell us the country has endorsed them, that the people have voluntarily approved of their

course. First, they tied the country hand and foot and then they issued a repudiation argument, and when the people endorsed them in reference to these things the government said: This is a full en-dorsation of the whole scheme. The same methods were employed to some extent in 1908. Last fall we again had the frantic appeal that we should again put my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in to finish his work. I do not say that in a sense it was not perhaps good party politics of my hon. friend to lie low and say nothing about this loan, but I question the honesty of that procedure. When we know that Mr. Hays' letter asking for this loan was dated only November 16, I think we are absolutely justified in believing that this was a compact, if not signed, sealed and delivered, at least thoroughly understood between the right hon. gentleman and the Grand Trunk Pacific; and although it is true that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was too astute to acknowledge that there was such a compact, he was also too honest to deny that there was a compact.
The right hon. gentleman cannot be allowed to congratulate either himself or his party on a scheme of this kind. I do not believe he has shown the great and prudent statesmanship he might have shown in connection with this whole matter, but rather that he has woefully failed to rise to a real sense of his duty to the people of Canada. In this I do not say that I am voicing the opinions of hon. gentlemen opposite or even all of my friends on this side, but I say from my own point of view that at that time Canada was at the parting of the ways, and while some people do not share my views, I say that, having evolved a great scheme for a transcontinental railway from ocean to ocean which included the principle of government ownership in the eastern section, the 'right hon. gentleman displayed a grievous lack of foresight in not applying that principle to the whole road, adopting it from ocean to ocean. In 1904 I campaigned for five long months on this ground, and on the programme of the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) of government ownership from ocean to ocean being infinitely preferable to the bargain the government have made, and from the extreme north to the extreme south of the immense riding which I have the honour to represent I obtained an enthusiastic response. More than that, had my election come on on the same day as other elections 1 would have won out hands down on that very appeal for government ownership. Hon. gentlemen here know that what I might call almost a scurvy trick, at all events a shady trick was played in deferring the election, yet in spite of that and in spite of the fact that the government had been sustained all through the
country, I was defeated by so small a majority that a change of one vote in each polling place would have elected me. Therefore when my right hon. friend and the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Finance and other gentlemen on the other side of the House talk of optimism and of faith in our country, I would like to see them extend their optimism and faith a little further. There is at this moment no subject which is so agitating the public mind and which is of such importance in the development of democratic government in this country as the great question of public franchises, and I say that it is a true patriotism which not only looks out for to-day but studies the needs of the country for years to come. Those who embrace Socialism in many cases are driven to it from the multiplication of millionaires whose wealth comes from the unearned increment and the sweat and toil of others to which they have not contributed. We have great abuses in our industrial system to-day and I do not say that these abuses would be solved by the appropriation of the wealth of individuals by the State. I do not believe that any State has the right to kill private initiative. There must be room for private enterprise and a man is entitled to what he justly earns, but I would point out that we are having daily forced home the necessity of the people of the country owning its great public franchises. Public ownership of this great Transcontinental Railway system need not necessarily mean government operation. It did not involve government operation as my right hon. friend knows m respect of the eastern section, although here again I say I have perhaps felt greater faith than some of my friends in government operation. I admit that it is practically impossible to have successful government operation of large industrial enterprises as long as our government operations are riddled by party politics, but it is a want of faith to say that successful government operation is impossible. We could eliminate partyism and employ in government work only men who are thoroughly trained and thoroughly capable of discharging the duties devolving upon them, not simply hack politicians, reaping their reward for party services. I say that the principle is fundamentally and eternally right, and to assert that the people of Canada are not capable of carrying out this principle in their national life is not to display courage and patriotism but something quite the reverse.
Speaking of the loan which is now before the House, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) have said that the Grand Trunk Pacific can sell their own bonds at about 90 cents on the dollar, and yesterday they said that therefore the margin of 10 per cent is practically all the money on which we are running any risk

or on which we could sustain any loss. Why should we saddle ourselves with more debts? Why should we pay out great sums in commissions and brokerage to save the pockets of the people who already owe the country $15,000,000 of capital to say nothing of interest? If either claim is true it would be almost better to pay the Grand Trunk Pacific people that ten per cent margin and have done with it. Why was not that proposition made, in order that we should at least know the limits of our obligations? We all know, it has been pointed out in unmistakable terms, that this loan practically means that we shall repay the Grand Trunk people $7,000,000 expended for the Grand Trunk Pacific. This company already owes us an immense amount and its chief men are in various ways making immense fortunes out of this work without advancing any money and without taking any risks. The Grand Trunk Railway, by guaranteeing one-quarter of the bonds, receive $25,000,000 worth of stock for which apparently they do not give one dollar's worth of cash or its equivalent. The contract of 1903 contained a clause practically compelling them, if they took that $25,000,000 worth of stock, to give cash or the equivalent of cash. On page 11203 of 'Hansard' of 1903 we have these questions:

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask the minister a question? Will he tell us how the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to build branch lines and buy rolling stock by giving away their stock to the Grand Trunk Railway Company?
They cannot give it away. They must get cash in exchange for it. The very face of the contract shows the untenable position which my hon. friends take.

The hon. gentleman overlooks the fact that the contract says that the Grand Trunk Railway Company must get at once the whole $25,000,000. If they get the whole $25,000,000 at once, how is the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway going to use that to build the railway?

My hon. friend supplies the obvious answer. The answer is because the Grand Trunk Railway will pay for it and give the money. My hon. friend supplies the answer to his whole argument.
At that time, then, these people, "3who were taking some little part in this project, were required for that $25,000,000 of the common stock to give its full equivalent, either in cash or in some other valuable form ; and yet in the cloudy and ambiguous amendments made since, they have been relieved of that obligation, and they get the $25,000,000 of common stock for no value except the guarantee of the bonds.
The reason I have so little sympathy for the Grand Trunk Pacific people is that they are making money out of this project in a Mr. BURRELL.
variety of ways. Besides the assistance we are giving them, they are making money through their townsite company, in the marvellous way in which railway companies always make money out of the unearned increment. This has been well shown by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Mid-dlebTo), who said, at page 4188 of 'Hansard' :
We find that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company hands over all its town sites to a separate company called the Grand Trunk Pacific Town Site and Development Company. I find that the directors of this company are C. M. Hays and friends. There are thirty thousand shares of stock in this Grand Trunk Pacific Town Site and Development Company. The directors, according to the return brought down by the Minister of Railways, are C. M, Hays, E. J. Chambter-lin, William Wamwright, W. H. Biggar and E. H. Fitzhugh, all of them directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific also, each of whom owns two shares and has paid $200. That is to say, these five directors who have the management and control of the Grand Trunk Pacifio Town Site and Development Company have onlv invested $1,000, in the institution, which controls and owns eighty-one town sites between Winnipeg and Edmonton. The acreage is 78,640 acres. There we have that acreage, composed chiefly of town sites made valuable by the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, which we are financing, and these gentlemen who have only invested $1,000 are controlling the whole company. In addition to that, they own a three-quarters interest in the whole town site of Prince Rupert.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the reason why we are relieved of any feeling of sympathy for these men, who in various ways are making an enormous amount of money out of the people of this country.
What did they pay for the townsites?

I have not the figures, but I know that they did not pay very much for those in British Columbia. For Prince Rupert, I think they paid something like $2.50 an acre; but we made a much better bargain than the Federal government, because we retained one-fourth for the people of British Columbia.
This company have been astute enough to see that the government and the people of Canada are kept off their most valuable asset, namely, the branch lines and the terminals. In the contract of 1903, we have this paragraph:
35a. A mortgage which shall be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property, tolls, rights and franchises of the company, including all equipment and property to be thereafter acquired by the company (but not including branch lines exceeding six miles in length or the revenue therefrom or the franchises in connection

therewith, or such additional rolling stock as may, with the assent of the government, be designated and marked by the company as constituting the equipment thereof, and not including ships or any municipal or provincial grants of land, by way of bonus or subsidy, to the said company for other than railway purposes) to secure the payment of the said issue of first mortgage bonds guaranteed by the government.
That is to say, they give us a security, but when they give it they take care to keep out of it all the good and tangible assets. Contrast that with the bargain made by the Conservative government with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which our friends opposite talk so much about. In that case the company threw in every branch line and every terminal they had, as security.
In the face of these facts my own feeling is-and I am voicing the feeling of a large number of the people of western Canada, that if this loan must go through, if the government have neglected, as I believe they have, the true interest of the country, these people should give some adequate security for the loan. It is not a" case of an eye for an eye, of stock for stock, or anything of that sort. We Conservatives believe in giving help when it is necessary and there is just reason for giving it; but if we are to be the bankers of this institution, let us behave as bankers should. If we pledge our credit for them, let us hold that common stock as security until they have paid their debt. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has rightly said that the needs of the great west are obvious to the government. We believe that it is the duty of the government to think twice before handing out in this lavish way the moneys of the people of this country without seeing that the just needs of the people are met. I will conclude by emphasizing the fact that we in the west believe in this road, we want to see it assisted where that assistance is necessary and justifiable, we want to see it extended in every reasonable and just way, but we hold that when that is done the rights and interests of the taxpayers of this country should be safeguarded. This is the position which I placed before the electors of my constituency, and which was endorsed by them in the strongest possible way, and I do not hesitate to place it before this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. A. LANCASTER (Lincoln and Niagara).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to repeat the arguments that have been made on this side of the House as to the improvident nature of this proposed loan-improvident from the point of view of the people of Canada-which I am afraid the government have overlooked; but I wish to
emphasize one or two aspects of the question which have struck me. The bargain which was made by the government representing the people in 1903, and modified in the interest of the company in 1904, it has been said was approved of by the country in the general election following. But I wish to emphasize here a matter that he touched upon but did not go into quite as fully as he might have, probably because he was not in the House at the time. It was only two years after that second bargain, that the most profitable part of the undertaking was deliberately put in the name of another institution so that it would not be liable for the obligations which either the Grand Trunk Railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific had assumed in those two contracts that the people were supposed to have passed on in the elections of 1904. The Act to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines company came up in this House in 1906. I opposed it, and so did other hon. gentlemen, in the Railway Committee and in this House, but it was voted through by the government and its supporters, notwithstanding the faqt that they practically made no reply to the objection that those branch lines, which were to be the main source of revenue and profit and I may say of solvency, in the case of these companies with which we had contracted, were being put in the name of another institution, thereby avoiding entirely the obligations which the people of Canada had against the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway. After the two bargains had been made in 1904 and 1903, which my constituents and myself considered bad bargains for the country, the next serious thing done was the establishing of that company for the construction of branch lines, and thus relieving those branch lines, which are to be the great source of profit to the main line, from any liability for the obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway or the Grand Trunk Pacific. Following that concession, I was surprised to learn this session that the government proposed to advance the Grand Trunk Pacific $10,000,000 more. What was always the contention of the government ? They said : ' If you will give these companies all they ask, they will certainly be able to give you profitable railway transportation for the people.' And they put through this most unbusinesslike and purely philanthropic legislation in order to remove all possible danger and doubt of these companies not being able to carry out their obligations. The intention then was that by this legislation regarding the construction of the branch lines, we would make it certain that, these lines would be speedily built and the much desired transportation facilities afforded. But we find to-day that none of those lines have been built, and that nothing has been done ex-

cept that we have paid out a lot of money. We find that the Grand Trunk Railway has been getting all the benefit without giving any actual value in return, but simnly acting as the endorsers of the Grand Trunk Pacific. We find that the Grand Trunk Railway has been allowed to get stock in the Grand Trunk Pacific in return for their mere endorsation, just as a broker would charge for lending his name to enable some one to raise a loan, without giving any actual value. The government have acted on the assumption that the whole benefit to this country, which this country need expect, consists in hurrying up the completion of all the transportation facilities required and supposed to be served by the construction of this railway. Having in view the great concessions which we ?ava in 1903 and 1904, no one expected that any attempt would be made to incorporate the branch lines under any other name than that of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Let me point out that everv opnortunity was given the government to protect the people by adding a condition in the Act incorporating the branch lines company?, which would make these branch lines subject to the same obligations as the parent company. I urged that in the railway committee: and when the Bill came back from that committee, I had the temerity to move an amendment providing that that charter should not in any way impair the security or lien of this government, but that the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch lines should be held liable with regard to the branch lines in exactly the same way as it was in the original contract. The amendment was objected to by the government, and the Bill passed without that protective clause. On the third reading of the Bill, I felt it my duty to move the six month hoist, but that also was voted down, and the government passed the Bill regarding the branch lines without any protection to the people.
On this side we have always contended that if we are to provide practically nine-tenths of the cost of the railway, we might as well own the railway. If the people had believed in 1904 that that railway was going to cost what we then contended it would, and what time has proved it will cost, there is not the slightest doubt that the government would have been swept out of power. But the people said :	' We
have the word of the Prime Minister that it will only cost $13,000,000.' Campaign literature of the government had on its front page in large letters the inscription: 'A new Transcontinental Railway for $13,000,000', and it also contained the statement of the Prime Minister, who had made the bargain and claimed to know all about it and whose Minister of Railways (Mr. Mr. LANCASTER.
Blair) had left this cabinet because he differed from them on that question, that the road would be built for $13,000,000. The people believed that we were entirely wrong, that we were unduly afraid, that we were the victims of our imaginations, and relied on the pledge of the Prime Minister, circulated in all his campaign literature, that they would get this Transcontinental Railway for $13,000,000. They had not then the slightest idea that these branch lines would be taken away from our security, that the security of the people would be impaired by the building of these branch lines by another company. Now, what do we find ? Either the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway are riot able to carry out their contract with the people or else they are able and are asking for $10,000,000 as a gift. One thing or other must be the case. If they cannot carry out their contract, if they cannot build the road with all the assistance given them, with all the legislation passed entirely in their interests and upon a basis which would not be dreamed of in any other business transaction-if they cannot, with all these advantages, build the railway, what ought we to do? We ought to let them default and then take over the railway ourselves and own it and operate it or lease it to somebody else.
It is contended that this railway policy of the government will be of great advantage to the country because the earnings of the railway will be great and the traffic enormous. Let me submit this point. We are here to make a bargain for the people, and I concede that we must not be mean in doing it or pessimistic or afraid of the future of our country. Now, the Grand Trunk Pacific either can carry out the contract without this $10,000,000 or they cannot. If they cannot, they are no railway builders, and we can find somebody else who will build that road on better terms. The Grand Trunk Pacific contended that in 1903 and 1904 that with the assistance then given them they could carry out the work. Were they deceiving us then? Were they not honest in making us believe that, with the assistance then given them and the additional assistance which they got in being allowed to build branch lines free from the obligations they had originally incurred, they could complete the road. If they were not, we ought not to lend them this $10,00,000. If they were then honest, they are not entitled to this loan, because they do not understand their business. Take the other alternative, if they can build this road without this $10,000,000, why not let them do it, or borrow the money somewhere else. Why should Canada give them this money and lead them to believe that all they have to do is to come to the government and say :
