' We need the money and because you have already incurred such large, obligations, you must give us all we want more.'
Now, not to detain the House at too great length, in view of the fact that these matters are not answered seriously by any one upon the government side, in view of the condition in which this debate is at this moment-that, notwithstanding what was said in regard to the resolution by hon. members of the opposition, from our respected leader down, there is no answer to these propositions or suggestions as to the improvident nature of this loan, I am not prepared to vote (speaking for myself and my constituents) for the second reading of the Bill. For, as the Bill stands, there is no protection in it, and I am afraid that if I were to declare myself as voting for the second reading, it might be said by some that I had been willing to adopt the principle of the measure, and the principle is all wrong if it is to be judged by the arguments that have been used up to this time. If we have to throw more money into this deal, then it simply means that we have to pay for this whole road from Moncton to the Pacific. Under these circumstances, we ought not to grant the loan. As the effect of this is that we must pay for the road, it will be much better for the government to own it and either operate it or hand it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific or some other institution to operate it on rental. This would be much better than going on with this legislation that we now have before us.
. Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
BORDEN What is the estimate of the Minister of Finance as to the actual cost to the country by way of interest on the loan which will be necessary for the purpose of raising this money?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is difficult to determine that to a fraction. Our last loan, as stated here, cost us a shade over four per cent. By the way, I notice that to-day an hon. gentleman not only quoted that at a shade over four per cent, but added various charges. Of course, four and a fraction covered the charges referred to. If this loan were placed on the market at this moment, we might have to pay four per cent, but I think the probability is that we can get it a shade less. I think the tendency of the money market is rather downard, and our next loan should be on somewhat better terms than the last.
When quoting four per cent, does the hon. minister mean the nominal percentage or the interest including expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In quoting four and a fraction, that meant the unit rate. 1 think we ought to realize a shade better. That will depend on the condition of the market.

If it is a banking transaction, why should there be any doubt about it?
ME FIELDING. There is no doubt about the rate we are to charge.

I am aware of that. But there is certainly doubt as to whether that rate will indemnify the country. This is a banking transaction, and bankers usually get in deposits at a certain rate and lend them out at a higher rate. I am not disposed to press that argument unduly in this respect, but surely it is a fair proposition that the country ought to receive as much interest as it pays. If there is any doubt, as there seems to be-and the doubt entertained by others may be greater than that entertained by the Minister oi Finance-I should think that some provision might be embodied in the Bill which would make that absolutely certain and which would thoroughly safeguard the country against any loss in respect of the interest on this loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is hardly necessary. It is desirable there should be a fixed and definite rate on the loan, and that should be made, as nearly as may be, the rate that will guard against loss. I think it is just as likely that this rate will show a profit as that it will show a loss. We take that risk. I think that in the present tendency of the money market we are not likely to pay more than four, and the probability is as strongly in favour of our getting it' at less.
As I understand it, the government will actually have to borrow the money before it will lend-the transaction oi borrowing will have to be completed before lending commences?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As soon as the preliminaries are settled, we should begin to use money out of existing funds if any are available. But that we would later make good, so, practically the answer to the hon. gentleman's question would be * Yes.' The government moneys all go into a general fund. If anything is taken from that general fund for this purpose, steps must be taken to replace it.
Is it not probable that the minister will not be acquainted with the effective rate of interest per unit prior to the time he will be called upon to pay out the first instalment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Possibly not. If our finances generally were in condition to allow it, we would pay them the money the

moment they comply with the provisions of the Act. But, immediately, we should have to borrow it, and so the two transactions go together.
Mr. AMES'. Has the minister taken any steps to float a new loan having this in view?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No formal steps have been taken, but we are watching the money market and intend to take the steps when the proper moment arrives.
The minister will watch his chance, and, when he sees the proper moment has arrived, will float a new loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will watch the money market and will seize the most favourable moment for making the loan, as in the past.

If, before the loan is finally disposed of, there is some financing to be done, as there was in the case of the Quebec bridge, and we pay a higher rate than four per cent, is this going to be charged to the Grand Trunk Pacific? It is probable that the moment the statute is passed the money will be sought for by the construction company. It is not probable that we could get money at four per cent, but shall be obliged to pay more than that. Speaking, generally, would it not be better for this section to be so framed that the country would recoup itself, as bankers do, from the loan to the railway company the whole amount of interest that we are obliged to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then, we should have to associate with that the provision that, in the event of our borrowing the money on more favourable terms, we would give them back the difference.
Why ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have the suggestion of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that we should charge exactly what it costs us.

I could understand that, for the purpose of negotiating a loan, the rate must be fixed by statute-at least, I conceive that that is possible. In connection with the question put by my hon. friend from St. Antoine, Montreal, (Mr. Ames), would it not be possible to ascertain what are the whole charges to which we are going to be subjected? What are the accidents of the loan, so to speak, so as to fix the rate we shall absolutely require?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think it would be possible to ascertain definitely. If this legislation were completed immediately, and the Grand Trunk Pacific were to comply with the requirements of this statute respecting the mortgage and Mr. FIELDING.
so forth, and if we had the money in hand, there is no reason why we should not give them that money instantly. But of course, we should have to include it in our borrowing powers, borrowing at the market rate. I think the situation is such as enables us to say that we are just as likely to borrow at a shade below four per cent, as we are to pay four per cent, or about.

There is no necessity for settling the rate of interest the moment the first advance is made to the company. The company want the money as soon as- they can get it, and they have to pay the interest on it semi-annually. Consequently, the first interest payment will not be due until six months after the first instalment is advanced, and in the course of those six months the government can tell exactly what that money has cost to raise; consequently they could without difficulty bill the company at that rate, the rate it actually costs to get that money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it would be more satisfactory to have a fixed rate, leaving no doubt whatever, and in fixing that rate we have estimated that we will be able to borrow money at four per cent. I have a decided opinion that we are quite as likely to borrow at a shade below four per cent as above; and therefore the company is taking as much risk as we are.
Judging from past experience, the company is likely to get the best of that gamble. I think we should protect ourselves.
From the minister's experience of loans, about how much will it cost to float this loan of $10,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We don't stop to consider what the expenses are, only to get the net result. When I say four per cent, I think that will cover all expenses. In fixing the cost of a loan we include all expenses. I am assuming it will cost four per cent, it may be a fraction above four per cent, but it is just as likely to be below, in which case the company takes the risk.
I think there was a return brought down some time ago which showed that it cost for floating loans somewhere between two and three per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are expressed in net rates in each case.
I think an answer was made in the House that it cost us two or three per cent to float certain loans.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Our loans cost us, as respecting the chief items exactly what they have been costing us for many years. But there is now a new item which adds ma

terially to the charge, that is, the item of underwriting, which is about 11 per cent. We think that while that has to appear as a part of the cost of the loan, we get a benefit in the better prices we obtain through that operation. Yet it has to appear as a part of the cost of the loan, just as in some past instances discounts would have to appear as a part of the cost of the loan. 1 have no doubt that if a comparison were made between these loans it would be shown that the cost of our loans, broadly expressed, is not greater than it has been in former years, except for this new condition which has arisen, that is, the item of underwriting, which must include brokerage in connection with the underwriting. The broker meets you at every door when you endeavour to place a loan, and the charge for the underwriting, and the brokerage in connection with the underwriting, amounts to 11 per cent. That is, in that sense, a new charge which did not exist in former years, because the conditions of the money market did not require it. But while we have to account for that as a charge, in reality it is not a burden to us, because we are satisfied we get a benefit for it in the better price which is fixed by the underwriters. For illustration, in our last loan we had to come to an agreement with the underwriters as to the price. Naturally we wanted the best price we could get, and naturally the underwriters would like the price to be as low as we would be willing to make it. So after careful discussion we agreed upon a price, and it turned out that that price was higher than the public in the money market was willing to pay, and when the loan was offered to the public, only 41 per cent of it was taken up at that price, because the ordinary public investor thought we had fixed our price too low. But the underwriters had to guarantee it to us. And so we got the benefit. Although this is a new charge, it is not a new burden to us, because we are satisfied we get the benefit of that in the higher price we are able to obtain.

The minister does not meet my point. I am not concerned to know whether we are better or worse off in borrowing than under a former government. The minister says that the underwriting and brokerage are a new item, and that it costs 11 per cent. Now, will the minister tell us what the former cost was before this new item was added?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would have to turn to the contract we have with our financial agents. But I will at a later stage give the hon. gentleman the information. It is already on the table of the House, in a return.
The minister tells us that as a matter of fact his underwriting cost 11 per cent. Now would the other branch of the expense be equal to 11 per cent, less or more, speaking generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is not as much as that, but I would not like to answer definitely. I would rather give an exact statement.
It would be decidedly less than 11 per cent.
Would it be as much as one per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be materially less than 11 per cent.

Supposing we take it as 1 per cent, fox the purpose of my argument, that would represent in all 2 per cent that it would cost to float a loan. _ But the return brought down showed, I think, that there was a considerable expense in connection with the floating of these loans. But we have suffered a good many disappointments already in connection with this railway, and I do not feel any great confidence in the statement made this afternoon that this will be a net expense of 4 per cent, including the expense by way of floating the loan. If the minister has brushed that item aside as immaterial, even if it cost 2 per cent to float that loan, of course it would represent $200,000 upon this transaction, and if not included in that 4 per cent, it will mean a net loss to Canada of $175,000 or $200,000. I think the least the minister should do is to make perfectly sure that we at least should not be losing money by this transaction in the way of interest.
It is a very easy thing to arrange that whatever rate of interest we pay we shall at least be recouped for that amount. It is right enough to provide for the payment of four per cent, but there should be a supplementary provision that if it costs more the country will not be put to a loss. Every step in this transaction that we have taken since the day when the Prime Minister first made the announcement of this legislation has been a disappointment to the country. Every amendment made has been an amendment by which the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific have benefited and by which the country has suffered and has been put to loss. Therefore, it is very little to ask that it shall be made absolutely clear that if it costs us more than four per cent- and the position that Canada is now in as regards the money market does not make it unlikely that it will cost more than four per cent-we shall be recouped by the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I see the matter in a different light from my hon. friend both as regards the contract generally and as respects this transaction. When I state the probable rate of interest I am including the expenses of every kind. The rate will include what we will have to pay for brokerage, printing and the various incidental charges. What precise rate they may ask us we do not know, but we know as respects the past and there is no reason to suppose that it should be more in the future. If, a few months ago, when we went to the money markets, when the conditions were more severe than they are at the present moment, we were able to borrow money at a shade over four per cent, which is probably the net rate of our last loan, is it not reasonable to suppose that another loan, with an improving market, may probably be obtained at a cost of four per cent? But while I state that as a reasonable proposition, I also state frankly that we have thought it best that we should take a measure of risk on both sides, that we should fix a definite rate of interest in the expectation that we would be able to borrow the money at that rate and at perhaps a shade less. If it costs us a shade more we take that risk to the extent of what we pay in addition.
Wliat risk will the company take?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we borrow the money at three and a-half per cent and charge them four we may make a profit out of it.
Why not make it a matter of certainty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We think it desirable to make it a matter of certainty as to the rate which they shall pay, but not as to the rate at which we shall borrow the money at some time in the future. That is why we take the risk.

When the Minister of Finance says that it is reasonable to suppose that the condition of the money market will be less stringent he does not refer to the fact that the position of Canada as regards the borrowing of money is not likely to improve for a exeat many years to come. The fact that Canada is going so heavily into the borrowing business and so frequently, that the minister will have, in all probability to take a trip to England immediately this session is over, and that we will be constantly on the borrow for the next 'few years will probably far more than counteract any improvement in the money market. So, I think I might say, by way of prediction, against the experience of the minister in the borrowing of money, and he has had a great deal of experience in that respect, that it will not be found that we can effect better terms in
the near future than we have done in the near past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will not predict. I think there is a fair chance of it, but we will get the best terms that we can get in the money market. That is all I promise to the committee.

I do not see why we should be discussing the question of a gamble and risk being taken either by one or the other. This company comes to us for a loan. We should fix the rate of interest. We are under no obligation to the company. We are stepping in where they should have remained. We are getting in under the burden that they should have shouldered and which, according to the first contract, they inevitably would have had to shoulder, which it was intended they should shoulder, and which the right hon. Prime Minister and three of his ministers declared they would shoulder. Now, we let the Grand Trunk out from having provided for a certain sum of money for the construction of the prairie section. We are repaying them that money. We are under no obligation to them. Why should it be a matter of risk between either party? The country should not risk anything. We should have a rate of interest which would make the country absolutely secure and we should charge them what we think would carry that amount. We should charge them such per cent as we pay for the loan, including all costs of charges. I would ask the minister whether he proposes to make a special ten year loan to cover this $10,000,000 which is to be repaid in ten years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would think not. I would like to have a free hand to do what is best, but I do not at present anticipate such a course.

Is this $10,000,000 that we are lending to the Grand Trunk Pacific to be expended yet upon the road or is it the purpose of the $10,000,000 loan to pay back to the Grand Trunk what they have already expended on the road?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will pay it to the Grand Trunk Pacific upon the certificate of an engineer in the usual way. As a matter of fact, I understand that the Grand Trunk have advanced moneys which have gone into the Toad and in that way they will be recouped. We will only pay upon the evidence of an engineer in the usual form that this money represents work which has been done on the road.
My hon. friend knows, I suppose, as a matter of fact, that a very large proportion of the $10,000,000 has already been expended and payment made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been advanced by the Grand Trunk.
And payment made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. But we have no certificate of it. We can only pay this money on the engineer's certificate that the work has been performed.
This money will not he paid for rolling stock or anything of that kind? It will be paid for the actual construction of the road bed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Will the loan for which this money will be paid out be made as to time according to this, loan? Will you flcat a ten year loan in order to pay this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said to my hon. friend from North Toronto that while I desire to have a free hand to do whatever is best in view of the condition of the money market I do not at the present time contemplate a ten year loan. I would anticipate that the loan would be foT a longer period.

If the minister makes a thirty or fifty year loan and agrees to pay the present high rate for fifty years in order that he may accommodate this company for ten years he may have to pay this increased rate of interest for many years after the loan to the company ceases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend puts in words to which I object. He says at this rate. We do not necessarily propose to pay this rate. The fact that we raise the money, if it be deemed expedient to raise it, as part of a loan extending over fifty years, would probably help us to get it at a better Tate. If the market condition is such that a fifty year loan is expedient and if that would help us to get a lower rate then, we should be free to take advantage of that condition.

If we negotiated a thirty or a fifty year loan at three and four-fifths per cent in order that we might be able to accommodate these people for ten years we would be bound to pay three and four-fifths per cent for thirty or fifty years when probably before that time we will be able to get cheaper money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That does not follow. I have no doubt that at the expiry of that 10 years, when the money is repaid, the government of Canada will find abundant uses for it and we will suffer no loss.

Would not the simplest manner be for the government to float a special ear-maTked issue of $10,000,000 of bonds at the best rate they can get and to say to the company: ' Whatever the money costs us for the ten years you want it, you must pay us? ' The government should simply act as their bankers in this particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think it would be wise to float a ten year loan unless the market conditions for the moment seemed to make that the proper course to take. I think it better to look at the market conditions and issue the loan in the manner and for the term and on the conditions that will give the best results. If it proves a satisfactory rate, we will be the gainers.
I am ^strongly of the opinion that there is a greater probability of our getting the money a shade below four per cent than above it; but I will not prophesy, we will get the best rate we can.
I think the minister has nearly exhausted his power of prophesy on this railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
And I do not think he can complain if some one on this side should offer one casual remark on that line.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not complain.

This is an accommodation, it cannot be put on any better ground by the government, we are accommodation endorsers for this Tailway. The very easiest terms on which a neighbour accommodates his friend is that he shall not lose one cent, unless the person for whom he endorses becomes bankrupt. He may exact as a condition of endorsement a percentage for the accommodation, but at least he will insist on not losing on his advance. That is the position which we should be in in this matter. The government ought to make definite arrangements for four per cent with a supplementary condition that in no event shall this loan entail loss upon Canada. This loan should be kept distinct so that we could know in the end exactly where we come out on the transaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will know next session what it will cost us, as we will have to replace it by another loan.

We ought to know now what we are going to pay and it should be kept distinct. That, however, is not a sine qua non, the main point is that we should not lose by this loan. As was stated by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), we understand that the Grand Trunk Railway Company allege that they have loaned $7,000,000 of this money and it is alleged that that $7,000,000 has been put into the road. The minister says that he will ascertain definitely that that money has been put into the road. I take it that the minister will do that but supposing that that $7,000,000 has been put into the road, then there will be left only $3,000,000 available for new work. Does the minister know how much it will take t# complete the prairie section? In other

words, will $3,000,000 of new money put into it complete the road?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At an earlier stage, in introducing the resolution, I gave in very full detail the figures which were designed to show that this $10,000,000 to he applied in the way described will finish the prairie section. We have, of course, only the reports of the engineers in that respect and I am beginning to give engineer's estimates with a word of qualification.
If that is the case it would appear that the prairie section is within $3,000,000 of being completed. Does the minister believe that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the information I get from the engineers and I am bound to accept it in good faith.

I wish to be clear as to the application of the $10,000,000. From the statement brought down by the minister it seems that the $10,000,000 is to be used for the completion of the road and for the payment to the Grand Trunk Railway of seven million odd dollars which they allege they have advanced for the construction of the road. The' minister sent officers of his department who have inquired into this expenditure and this advance by the Grand Trunk Railway, so he must now be in a position to state whether that $7,000,000 was actually advanced by the Grand Trunk and used in the construction of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see that we are very much concerned now with that $7,000,|000, because we will not pay out one dollar of this $10,000,000 except upon the certificate of the engineer that that money is represented by work in the road. If, in the meantime, they have arranged with their bankers or the Grand Trunk Railway or any one else for that advance, I do not think we are much concerned. As to the $3,000,000 finishing the road, it is $3,000,000 in addition to other funds which are still available from the government guarantee. This amount, plus the other amount available from the government guarantee, we are advised will finish the prairie section.

The minister must concern himself as to whether the money is earned or not. His officers have examined the accounts and certified that this money has been expended upon the road. Surely we are entitled to the details of the expenditure of that $7,000,000? Grand Trunk Pacific say they want $9,500,000 to complete the prairie section. This is referred to the officer of the department and he says $10,500,000 is required. You split the difference at $10,000,000. What available assets have they? They have available assets of the bonds not yet sold and

of construction material which is available to the amount of $1,500,000, and they want to return this alleged advance of $7,100,000. The officers of the department certify that this has gone into the construction of the road. In what form wa3 this advance made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have nothing which earmarks that particular $7,000,000, and it does not strike me as of importance to us to so ear-mark it. What we want to have certified to us is that there is work to represent the money which they will claim from us. The Grand Trunk Pacific will file statements that they have done the work; we do not care where they get the money; it is not our concern. They claim they have done work representing a certain outlay. We will submit that to our engineers, who must certify to it; and if the work is there to represent it, I do not think we are concerned whether they got the money from the Grand Trunk Railway Company or from a bank. That is a matter of their own arrangement. The vital point with us is to see that the work is there, and then the money is paid out only on the certificate of our own engineer that the work has been done.

The government has already agreed to advance $13,000 per mile on the 916 miles of the prairie section, amounting to $11,908,000; and we now propose to advance $10,000,000 more, making a total of $23,900 per mile, or altogether $21,908,000. Do I understand that the government will see that vouchers for that total amount are checked and passed as being for perfectly legitimate expenditures, and that when they reach that point their responsibility as to checking these accounts ceases, and any additional expenditure will not be subjected to the same examination?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend treats two funds as in a sense the same. One of these funds consists of the proceeds of the government guarantee, as to which the procedure is that the guaranteed bonds are issued and sold, and the proceeds deposited in a special ac'count in the bank to the credit of the Minister of Finance, separate and apart from our ordinary government revenue. This may be deemed trust money for the purposes of the railway. Not a dollar of that money can be drawn out until the government engineer has certified the accounts sent in as being correct, and only when he certifies that the claim is a proper and legitimate one against that money is any of it drawn. So much with regard to the government guarantee. With respect to the other transaction, which represents a portion of the money guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, inasmuch as they have

asked us for this loan, we have put it in the same position as our guarantee fund, and we say that this money must be drawn out only when the government engineer certifies that there is work to represent it.

The minister has not seen the point of my question. The govern-men are supplying $22,000,000 for the prairie section, which we will say will cost $32,000,000. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company are then obtaining $10,000,000 apart from the government. Is the government going to see that there is a careful audit of the whole $32,000,000, or only of the accounts they present up to $22^000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The audit covers the whole expenditure. Then it becomes a question of what proportion is chargeable on the guaranteed bonds and what proportion is provided by the Grand Trunk Company. But the audit of the Railway Department covers the total expenditure without any reservation.

Then do I underhand that the government will satisfy themselves, in respect to all the indebtedness that stands against "the road with respect to the first, second and third mortgages which are prior to our fourth mortgage, that every item which makes up those amounts has been carefully passed on by the government auditor, so that we may know that the government has taken the precaution to examine carefully every item of expenditure on the road, whether the government is to supply the money or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the audit of the Railway Department applies to the total outlay on construction.

With the minister's assurance, then, if next year we inquire how this $10,000,000 has been expended, we shall be permitted to travel in the same steps in which the auditor of the government has travelled, and examine the list of vouchers that make up the statements which the auditor has passed; so that what is now being done to satisfy the government that these expenditures are legitimate may be ratified by a committee of this House at the next session if it is so desired?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not changing the system in the slightest degree by this Bill. I am advised that the auditor of the Department of Railways does take into view all the expenditure on the road which are charged to construction account, and certifies that they are fair and proper and reasonable, and then a certain portion is charged to one fund, and a certain portion to the other. But all are subject to the audit of the department.

Then do I understand that a committee of this House will be permitted next session to travel in the same steps as the auditor and accountant of the Department of Railways in order to be assured that the whole of the $32,000,000 has been legitimately expended?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are making no change whatever in the system or in the terms of the contract, whatever they are; but my impression is that the audit of the Department of Railways is as broad as my hon. friend suggests. If I find that I am mistaken, I will qualify my statement at a later stage of the discussion.

The hon. gentleman knows that we were permitted to examine as trust funds how the first portion of the $13,000 per mile was expended. Do I understand that this $10,000,000 being in the same position, we shall be entitled to check over the amounts which are paid out as part of this advance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The contract is not varied in the slightest degree by this Bill. The moneys can only be drawn after government audit, and in the manner I have described. But I will read in ' Hansard ' what my hon. friend.has said and will discuss the matter with the auditor of the Railway Department, and if my answers have been too comprehensive, I will modify them.
This Bill is practically an amendment of the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It is to all intents and purposes, for it is putting the company in a better position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. We agree voluntarily to help them by way of a loan, but it is not an amendment to the contract. An amendment to the contract would have to be mutual.

At this time if we desire we can lay stipulations on the company, and if this matter is not clear, we can easily make it clear in this Bill.
Progress reported.
At Six o'clock House took recess.
After Recess.
House went again into committee on Bill (No. 110) respecting agricultural fertilizers.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. TEMPLEMAN (Minister of Inland Revenue).
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I move the reconsideration of section 6. My object is to move an amendment by adding sub-section:

(e) The materials from which the fertilizers were made.
What is the object of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: To give further information to the department. They already have to give the guaranteed analysis, and this is added.

Amendment agreed to.
Section 10 reconsidered:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This section provides that the purchaser of a registered fertilizer may send it to the department and have an analysis made on paying a fee of $5. It is suggested that this is too high a charge in case of farmers and others desiring an analysis, and I propose to reduce it to $1.

Amendment agreed to.
Section 15 reconsidered:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This provides for penalties. It says:
Every person who sells or offers or exposes for sale any fertilizer in respect of which the provisions of this Act have not been complied with

And so on. I propose to strike out the word 'person' and insert the words 'manufacturer or agent/
Would that include the storekeeper?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, I am bringing in another amendment to include the vendor. This applies to the party who gets the license to manufacture and guarantee the analysis.

Amendment agreed to.
Section 17 reconsidered:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I propose an amendment that will cover the point raised by the hon. member (Mr. Sharpe). It has been pointed out in the discussion that after a fertilizer is placed on the market with guaranteed analysis, some vendor might tamper with it by mixing with it inferior substances, thereby reducng its fertilizing value. I propose, after the word 'fertilizer' in the third line, to add the words:
-and every person who lowers the fertilizing value of a registered fertilizer by mixing any other substance therewith after said fertilizer has been placed upon the market by the manufacturer or agent.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I propose to add to this Bill the section, No. 21, as follows:
This Act shall come into force on the first day of January, nineteen hundred and ten.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: This will give the manufacturers time to conform to the Act. The season for fertilizers for this year is over.
A great deal of fertilizer is used in the fall of the year. Better make it 1st October.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: So far as the convenience of the department is concerned, 1st October would do as well as January 1, 1910. It might suit the trade better to begin with the year. It does not make much difference to the department.

But it makes a difference to the public, because a good deal of fertilizer is used in the fall in the Niagara district and elsewhere. It will be no more difficult for the manufacturers, but it will give the department control of the material sold for the fall season.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I move that it be made October 1, 1909.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
Bill (No. 127) respecting commercial feeding stuffs-Mr. Templeman-read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. TEMPLEMAN (Minister of Inland Revenue).
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This Bill is practically the same in all its details as the Bill which we have just passed, with the single exception that this is for commercial feeding stuffs, and the other was for fertilizers. The language is exactly the same except in those two words.
On section 2,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If it is a medicine it would not come under the Act. If it possesses nutritive as well as medicinal qualities it would. But if the contention of the correspondent is correct, and it is purely medicinal and not food, it would not come under the Act.

He does not claim it to be a medicine, but a tonic. I assume it is called a food because it contains preparations made from wheat which contain the protein and other elements of food. It is something in its effect like pepper, salt ginger, mustard. These are condiments,
they stimulate the stomach and make it secrete more gastric juice, and digest the food better.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Then it would not come under this section at all.
What would you put that under?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It would not come under any Act. It has to possess nutritive properties to be a feed as well as a medicine before it can come under this Act. If the statement of the correspondent is correct that this is purely a medicine and not a food it would not come under the Act.
I did not say that he claimed it to be a medicine. I said that it could more properly be classed as a medicine. He called it a condiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: And the manufacturer says that it is a food?
No, he says it is a condiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It would have to remain for investigation to find out whether it was a food under the Act or not. If it is a condiment or a medicine purely and simply it would not come under the Act, but if it is medicinal as well as nutritive it would come under the Act and very properly so because that is the object of the Act.
On section 4,
Name of foreign manufacturer's agent or representative in Canada to be filed with minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
That the section be amended by inserting after the word ' person,' in the 30th line, the word ' resident,' and after the word ' Canada,' in the 31st line, the words ' and acceptable to the minister.'
He said the point was raised in discussing the other Act that probably the agent might be an irresponsible person. I want to put that in as a safeguard.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 7,
Registration numbeT, how fixed; statement required.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
That the word ' importer ' in the 19th line he expunged.
He said:	The word 'importer' appears
and as the importer is not dealt with in the Act but simply the manufacturer or agent, I desire to expunge it.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 9,
Annual license to sell; fee; period of validity.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That the section he amended by inserting after the word ' obtained,' in the 2nd line, the words ' by the manufacturer or agent.'
Does this section mean that no one can sell any of these foods except he has a license, or has the license only to be taken out by the manufacturer?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The object of the Act is that the manufacturer shall take out one license himself, and that no commercial food stuff can be sold unless the manufacturer or the agent of the foreign manufacturer shall ta}ve out a license for that food stuff.
The section is not very clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think so. There is only one license to be taken out for each brand.
That is an annual license?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Yes.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 10,
Purchaser of registered feeding stuff may obtain analysis.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
There is a blank in the last line and I therefore move:
That the blank in the last line of clause 10 be filled in with the word ' one.'
Making it read one dollar.

How will it be with those parties all over the country who have a lot of feed on hand? The manufacturer will take out a license on the 31st December. There is a stock of these goods all over the country. Will the license taken out on the 31st December cover what is in the hands of the trade at that time, or will it only cover what the manufacturer or his agent sold after that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It might be necessary to introduce a clause to exempt stocks in the hands of vendors.

Otherwise you might do injustice to merchants and others.
On section 13,
Analysis in case of samples imported for personal use.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I propose making the fee in that case $5. The same amendment will apply in the case of analysis of food stuffs manufactured to the order of a purchaser.

The Act does not provide for the case of a foreign manufacturer who, without registering a resident agent imports a lot of feed materials, placing Mr. TEMPLEMAN.
them in the hands of merchants and having them sold without being registered. Who would then be liable under the Act?
That is material imported by the foreign manufacturer and sold under consignment?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We might amend
section 17.
The merchant is not an agent under the wording of the Act and the only suggestion I can offer is to make the merchant or person who sells an unregistered article liable under the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We could amend section 17 in that way.
On section 17,
Forgery of certificates, &c.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I would move to add the words ' and every person who sells an unregistered food stuff.'
That would cover the point. Would it not be well for the minister to amend the Fertilizer Act in the same direction?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We would have to have the amendment made in the Senate, and I will see if that can be done.

1 would also suggest that such fertilizer as Chilian nitrate, wood ashes and phosphates, sold in the commercial state, should be exempted in the same way as this Act exempts grains. For instance, it might be considered illegal for a person to buy Chilian nitrate by the bag and to sell it as such. I would like the minister to consider that.
On section 20,
Commencement of the Act.
I think that Act should come into force before the 1st of January next.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There is no objection to it coming into force on the 1st of October if the House thinks that the better time.

As against the manufacturer the Act should come into force at once, except as to the stocks now on hand, because the manufacturers all over the country are manufacturing and selling to the farmers fraudulent foodstuffs.
I think it would be wise to have the Act brought into force as quickly as possible. During the months of June and July an immense amount of food is purchased and consumed.

I would move that the date he changed to the 1st of July, 1909.
I might say that this foodstuff is a staple article which is sold daily. It is not something that a man need put in a stock of for a year, and there will be ample time for the dealers to get rid of all their stock before the 1st of next July. This is a matter that is pressing very hardly upon purchasers. The frauds in this class of food, as shown before the Agricultural Committee, are so great that drastic measures are necessary. The hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) and I have introduced Bills on this matter which this Bill now covers. It was ascertained before the Agricultural Committee that in a great majority of eases this commodity was made out of absolutely worthless stuff, such as sawdust and ground chaff and ordinary turf and moss, which were ground up and sold to the farming community as cattle feed. It is about time that this was stopped, because there is not 25 cents of food value in a ton of it. I would also suggest to the minister that something ought to be done to relieve the farmer of the duty of prosecuting the parties who wilfully break this law. The matter is now left in such an indefinite shape that there is no officer specially charged with the enforcement of the law. I pointed that out the other evening in the case of fertilizers and the objection is even greater in this case. The merchants are selling the farmers this foodstuff for cattle, which has no food value. We may run across cases where the purchaser gets an analysis made and finds a fraud has been committed on him, but he might not like to institute proceedings himself. Under the Adulteration Act, he would have to deposit $25 before any prosecution could be made. I do not see how the minister proposes to have the law enforced. Let him make it more easy to prosecute in such cases. Every few days we get circulars from the department showing "the results of analysis, but there is no prosecution. The circulars show that the articles are fraudulent but no effort is made to punish the guilty. Analysis of these foods have been made for years and the results sent out to the public in bulletins issued by the department, yet still these frauds are growing larger every day. I think the minister would do well to consider the advisability of inserting some provision which would enable an officer of the department, when he found there was a fraud, to lay the information before the magistrate. The minister said the other evening that it was the business of the department of Justice to prosecute. Possibly this department should in one sense be the prosecutor, but it would be much more effective to give an inspector the power to lav the information before a magistrate and file his certificate showing that an article put on the market was not up to the analysis printed on the package, and then have the manufacturer summoned to show why he should not be fined.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It would not be possible for the manufacturers of these commercial food stuffs to conform to the provisions of this Bill before the 1st of July, 1909. We require that they shall register, and take out a registered number, and put upon the packet a printed guaranteed analysis and other statements of fact. It would be scarcely fair to compel them to do this in that short time. I would be quite willing to have the Act come into force the 1st of October, 1909. Within that time they should be able to comply with it. With reference to the suggestion of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Currie) regarding prosecutions for violations of the Act, it is not the department who creates the standards but the manufacturers. The officers of the Department of Inland Revenue would procure a sample of every food-stuff on the market and analyse it, and if the analysis printed on the packet does not come up to that made by the department, the manufacturer can be punished under clause 15.

The department
undertakes to prosecute?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes. I move that the Act comes into effect the first of October, 1909.

I agree that the 1st of October would perhaps be early enough to have the law come into force. There is a considerable manufacture of food-stuff of medicinal qualities such as herbageum. I have in my desk analysis of that stuff and it is not worth as much as a food as ordinary linseed meal. It is composed of pure wheat meal, charcoal, sugar, &c. I do not wonder that the manufacturers of these protest and say they should not be compelled to put a label on the outside. If we have this Act come into force the first of October and then have it carried out, that will be time enough. The people have been defrauded a good many years and it is time to put an end to it.

There are thousands of samples which must be analysed and the department has not a sufficient number of analysts to doi the work between now and then. The work is very much behind now. Then you require to have the brands registered and licenses taken out and to make your own regulations, and all that will have to be done by the department within that time. Who is going to collect those samples for your analysts?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The department
does not make the analysis. It is the manufacturer himself who" will analyse and place a guaranteed anaylsis on the packet.
If he wants to give his food any standard, will he not require to have the government analyse it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The department does not guarantee the analysis at all. We would not allow any of our analysts to make the analysis. The manufacturer must have that done himself. Then the label on the package shows what nutritive value the food has. After it is put on the market, we have it analysed, and if the food is not up to the analysis labelled on the package, we take proceedings.
Suppose you want to prosecute, what is your evidence? There must be an analysis made, and there are not sufficient analysts in Canada to analyse the samples of food on the market at present.
I agree with what the minister says. This government must not be responsible for the analysis, but the manufacturer can get it analysed by any chemist he wishes.
Does the hon. member mean to say that any chemist in the city is fit to analyse itf

They certainly can get it done. As to the question raised by the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) that it would not be possible with the staff the minister now has to make these analyses in the time, would it not be much better for to to pay a few more officers for three or four months in order to bring the Act into effect all the sooner? Surely that would be better than to allow the farmers to be defrauded out of thousands and thousands of dollars. I think the first October is ample time for the manufacturers, and the saving to the people who buy these goods will be much greater than any possible cost in preparing for coming into force of the Act.

I do not believe there are a dozen manufacturers of these goods in the country that have not had their stuff analysed already by the government on one or two occasions. They all know the value of the analysis, though I think they will be slow to put the analysis given them by the government on their brand. As to giving them time, there is no need to be too lenient in this matter. Of course, hypothetical cases can be quoted. In the case of change in the custom law, which we make here in five minutes, there may be shown thousands of cases of people who have been injured by it, but we do not delay the law for that reason. I Mr. SPROULE.
do not see why we should be so awfully kind to these other people and give them so much time to load up the country with a few thousand more tons of this stuff. I do not wish to press the motion I have made, in opposition to the minister's wishes, because I would like to see this Bill go through without any contention. I think we should take the business view of this. If a business man had this in hand, he would bring this law into force at ten o'clock to-morrow morning. It is not going to hurt the small dealer, he may have some packages on hand, but, if he can show that he bought them before the change in the law-and his invoices will establish the facts of the case-there is not a magistrate in the country who will fine him.
_ Mr. SPROULE. I do not think the hon. member (Mr. J. A. Currie) knows much about the trade. You cannot find many respectable drug stores that do not manufacture this for themselves. They use linseed meal, ginger, antimony, sometimes shorts, bran or other material. Is everyone of these druggists to take out a license and get the feed analysed? They probably have a large stock on hand. It is not useless by any means. It is a food, a condiment, and a medicine, and it is good for cattle. There is a great difference between this and ground-up corn stalks or chopped straw. I can understand that all this trade can be brought under control. But, if you are going to do it in a short time, you will have quite a contract on hand. With three-quarters of the respectable drug stores all over the country to register and their products to be analysed, there are not enough analysts in Canada to analyse all these samples between now and 1st October.

The hon. member (Mr. Sproule) seems to think that the 'guaranteed analysis' must be the exact analysis of the contents. But, without an analysis, the man who makes the mixture can put on it a description as a 'guaranteed analysis' that will be safely within its value, and that will fulfil the requirements with relation to the guaranteed analysis.

What is the analysis for? It is to show the contents of the mixture. The analysis would have to be made by some one competent to go into the witness box and prove the case if called upon. Will any court accept the analysis of a druggist? Not unless he is also a qualified analyst, and not one druggist in fifty is a competent analyst. To get all these analyses made by the duly qualified people will take. time. I say, and I say advisedly, that there are not enough analysts in the Dominion of Canada to analyse all these samples of food between now and 1st October.

The hon. member (Mr. Sproule) may know of druggists who are mixing up these feeds, but the druggists in our vicinity do very little of it. We have the National Stock Food Company selling hundreds of thousands of dollars worth to these people. This concern advertises that it spends $200,000 a year in advertising its stuff. Who pays for all that?
I understand that it has been said that a great portion of this feed was made of ground corn cobs, and they are selling it by the train load. These are the people we want to get after. Very few druggists make their own, they handle other well known brands. In the stores you will see it piled up by the wagon load, and sold at these exorbitant prices. As I understand it, the manufacturer must register with the department and get his mixture analysed. Then, if he puts on the market a class of feed that does not come up to the standard given on the tag, prosecution will take place.

On motion for third reading,

I think it is an outrage upon the feed dealers that no provision
is made for the stock they have on hand. There are certainly thousands of tons of it
all over the country that are being sold today. Now every manufacturer who sells or exposes for sale any commercial feeding stuff after this Act is passed, is subject to a penalty. There is no provision made in the Act to let them sell what they have.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We give them four months in which to sell their stock on hand. The Bill will not come into force until the 1st of October. We have got to make a start some time. I do not know how we could make an exception for the stock at present on hand.
You did it in the Patent Medicine Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We provided that all stocks of drugs on hand, on the coming into force of the Act, should have a small label attached to them as provided by the department. But it seems to me that is not so necessary in this case. Holders of these feeding stuffs should be able to dispose of them during the next four ^months. I would also point out that it is the manufacturer or agent who is liable, not the vendor, for a contravention of that portion of the Act. The vendor is only responsible under the Act if he adulterates a food stuff already in the market. So I do not think the retail dealer will be hurt at all in selling any of his old stock, even after the Act comes into force.

Is he exempt? He is a manufacturer in every sense of the word under this Act. He has not taken out a license but he has a large quantity of this material on hand. He has only sold as much as is called for and he has to lose what he has on hand or sell it illegally. It is not the part of wisdom or fair play if you do not make some provision whereby these people may carry on their business in a legal way.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend must be referring to condiments or medicinal preparations rather than to feeding stuffs. There are very few druggists who would put up feeding stuffs in such quantities that they cannot dispose of them in four months. The Act does not apply to them unless they are foodstuffs proper. If any druggist has such a large quantity on hand that he cannot dispose of it before 31st December next he should come under the Act and be liable to its provisions.

Your Act provides that these compounds may be feeding stuffs, condiments and medicines. Take the prescription that I have spoken of again. Take linseed meal, bran, shorts and ground oil cake which are food stuffs. Put them with certain drugs and you have a preparation of foodstuffs and medicines combined. You sell them by the patent pail and they are ' valuable foodstuffs and medicines as well.

They will come under this Act. I have been so associated with the trade that I know very well how this is done. Take Orangeville, Shelbourne, Dundas, Flesher-ton, Markdale, Chatsworth and Owen Sound; you cannot go into any one of these places but you will find drug stores selling these goods and in most cases druggists manufacturing them. They will be selling them in violation of the Act under the provisions as contained here. They may decide to quit the manufacture of them in future but there is a lot of stuff that is not sold, they do not want to lose it and yet they do not want to sell in violation of the law.

In reply to my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) I think that these druggists are amply protected by this Act. There is no druggist of ordinary intelligence who cannot turn up the Pharmacopaea and in five minutes decide the food value of any of the ordinary articles that would be employed in a compound of this kind. He can turn up seed, meal, bran, &c., and ascertain their food values. Any man who is a druggist will very soon find out the food value of materials which are used to make up one of these articles and then all he has to do is to put a cerificate of the food and if he is going to give a false value to it let him put on a certificate for less than the actual value of the article. The analyst takes a sample of it, and sends it to the department and if it is found that the value of the article is five or ten per cent over, the guaranteed value I do not think the department would be inclined to prosecut the manufacturer. A man who undertakes to compound an article of this kind can very easily calculate the value of it from the means at his hand. I object to the length of time which is given for bringing this Act into force because there is no trade which has been treated with so much leniency as this. They have still five months to make up their minds what they will do and if they want to be safe they can tag their product with a statement of the food value really below the actual value. There is no misrepresentation if the value is greater. The hon. member for East Grey knows very well that there is no druggist in this country but who could very soon find out what food value there is in any article that he compounds or sells.

My hon. friend may be a travelling encyclopedia but he only exposes his limited knowledge when he says that it is only necessary to turn up the Pharmacopaea to find out the value of foodstuffs. Suppose that you went .to court on that what would happen? You cannot find an analysis of food in the Pharmacopaea. That would be absolutely valueless and the Mr. SPROULE.
druggist would be liable under the law if any person questioned the matter.

I think this is a good Bill, but there is one point in regard to which I do not think it goes far enough. If a manufacturer mixes a certain proportion of bran with middlings and grinds them together, thus reducing the food value of middlings, this Act would not touch him at all. The farmers have been complaining very much about the manufacturers mixing one of the lower grades made from the same grain, and thus decreasing the value of the article they are supposed to get. However, we may try this for a while and if it does not work satisfactorily we can amend it.

I think there is a great deal in the contention of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). This Bill, I understand, is a Bill to protect one class as against another class and in making legislation of this kind we should be very careful that no class is injured. I cannot agree with the position taken by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) in that he says that every druggist should be an analyst.
I did not say that he should be an analyst.

It is absolutely necessary to carry out the hon. gentleman's argument that he should be an analyst. But, it should be remembered that all druggists are not analysts. There are only a few in the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Inland Revenue. As the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has said, a man although he may be a very skillful chemist, may not be able to conduct properly an analysis of a food product. The hon. member's point is well taken that there may be thousands of pounds that the retail vendor has bought in good faith, and if he is not able to dispose of them before the time stated in the Act then the manufacturer of these goods becomes liable, although both he and the vendor have acted innocently and in good faith. For that reason I think that some provision should be made, just as in the case of the Act in regard to proprietary and patent medicines, whereby stocks on hand should be exempted from the operation of the Act or at least some further notice given. It is difficult for even a lawyer to keep track of all the changes made in the law from time to time. The druggists are a responsible class of the community, men f '>ood standing, men who are already subject to rigorous provisions of the law and I believe that some consideration and protection should be given them in introducing this law.

I quite approve of this very important legislation.

I believe it is in the interests of the farming community, as there is no doubt that farmers have been gulled by food stuffs which contained very little substance. For instance the manufacturers of pea meal for human food preserve the hulls of the neas, grind them up and sell them for cattle feed as pea meal, although they contain very little substance. Therefore it is of the greatest importance that these feed stuffs should be analysed and that the farmers should know the value and the strength of what they are purchasing. At the same time there is force in the argument of the hon. member for East Grev that the druggists may have large stocks of these goods on hand. There is little sale for them except in the spring and fall and large quantities are necessarily carried over. Injustice may be done to these druggists by cutting off the sale of their present stock in the fall. T think that the suggestion of my hon. friend is worthy of consideration.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.	.

Bill (No. 146) to amend the Act relating to Ocean Steamship Subsidies-Mr. Brodeur -read the second time, and House went into committee thereon. _
On section 1,

This section was adopted last year with the exception of the following changes. We provided that a contract should be made for the purpose of establishing a steamship line between Canada and France, and that we should pay a subsidy not exceeding $200,000, based upon the sum of $5,555 per trip. Last year the contract was made for one year only, because it was not known whether or not the French treaty would be adopted by the French authorities, and we thought that we could this year renew the contract for one year or for a longer period. But as the power which was given to the Governor in Council to make a contract had been exercised, the Department of Trade and Commerce were advised that they had no right to enter into another contract, and that it was necessary to obtain authority from parliament to do so. This Bill gives authority to the Governor in Council to enter into a contract or contracts with any person or company. It also provides that the subsidy shall be based on $6,666 per trip instead of $5,555. It is contem-lated to improve the service by putting on ships of 12 knots instead of 10 knots, as provided by the present contract.

In order that this change should come into effect, I think that the treaty with France should be ratified first, as the whole question of these subsidies depends upon the completion of our new arrangement with the French Republic. I quite approve of these new arrangements which we are making with the Allan Line, but subject of course to the confirmation of the treaty. That treaty at the present moment is an incomplete one, and under these circumstances I suggest that we cannot proceed with this Bill.

I do not think it would be fair not to enter into a contract for a large number of years at this time. It is true, the treaty has not yet been ratified by the French Chamber of Deputies, though it has been approved by the French Senate, before which it has been standing for more than a year. I have no doubt the Chamber of Deputies will also approve of the changes made in the treaty, because it has approved of the treaty of 1907, and because these changes are in accordance with public opinion in France. My hon. friend suggests that we should not enter into any contracts for the Mr. BRODEUR.
service even for this year so long as the treaty is not ratified. I cannot agree with him. The Allan Line has had that service established for several years.
Between what ports?

Between Havre, France, and Montreal and Quebec in the summer and St. John and Halifax in the winter. Many people were requested to avail themselves of the subsidy but would not do it, but in 1894 or 1895 the Allan Company agreed to take it up. They started the service and last year the subsidy was going to expire but we passed legislation providing for its renewal. Even if the treaty should not be ratified, I think we ought to provide for the contract this year because otherwise this service, which was established with a great deal of difficulty, would cease. It is expected, however, that the treaty will be ratified in May as soon as the Chambre des Deputes meets again.
Last year you paid $5,555 per trip. Did you have 15 trips?
I think so.

A service of how many
knots?
I think ten knots.
Were the vessels capable of running ten knots?
The contract provides for a ten knots service, and they must prove that they have furnished such service or they do not get the subsidy.
What were the results in the way of trade? We ought to know what we are getting for our money.
Last year the trade amounted to $10,000,000 or a little more.
How was that divided between exports and imports?
There were $8,000,000 odd imports and nearly $2,000,000 exports.
This is not the only line by which we get French goods into Canada.
It is mostly.
What has been the growth of imports from France in the last few years?

In 1905 the exports were $335,000, and in 1904 they had increased to $1,992,928. The imports were:
