1896		 2,810,000
1897		 2,651,000
1898		 3,975,000
1899		 3,889,000
I960	 4,368,006

I have not got the figures since. We expect to have larger exports because our exports have now to pay the maximum duty when the most of our competitors, such as Germany, Australia, Italy, Spain and Switzerland, export their goods to France under the minimum tariff, and there is a great difference between the maximum and the minimum. When the treaty is ratified, our trade with France ought to increase immensely, as our exports will get the benefit of the minimum tariff.

The French chambers and government have been at work some time revising their tariff. What is the general course of that revision? Is it towards raising the duties both in the minimum and maximum list against foreign imports?

The tariff in France is not submitted by the government itself but by a committee. I have seen somewhere that the French Senate are preparing a tariff, and that body is largely protectionist. It may be that the Senate committee would report strongly in favour of an increased tariff. But I do not know whether that same feeling exists in the lower House. I am under the impression that in the lower House the general feeling is in favour of more extensive commercial relations with other countries.

I would like to bring a few considerations to the attention of the minister. I suppose the government does not intend to put this subsidy into active operation for a period of years unless the French treaty is finally ratified.
Our intention is to make a contract for only one year, and after the treaty is ratified, we will make it for a longer term.

I have no objection to having the contract go on, so as not to break the connection. But I want to call the attention of the minister to two or three things that may happen in the future. In the first place, it is true that whatever may be the minimum tariff in France we will get the same rates under that minimum tariff that other favoured nations get. It is also true that if you put the minimum tariff up to a certain point, if it is a very high tariff, it precludes freedom of trade. It is not sufficient to say that it does not make any difference whether the minimum tariff is 25 per cent or 95 per cent, if we get the same advantage as others. In that respect that statement is true, but if it is a 95 per cent minimum tariff instead of a 25 per cent, it practically
precludes trade from outside countries. Now the other consideration is this:	The
French Chambers are revising their tariff, and from what I have seen in the newspapers it is probable that the tariff will be raised rather than lowered, and it may be that the minimum tariff will be brought up on a parallel, with the maximum, and that both of them will be raised. I think it would be the part of prudence not to make a contract for more than one year at the present time, until we see what the French tariff is going to be under its new form, because it might take such a basis in heightened minimum duties that it would not be worth while for us to spend $2,000,000 in order to cultivate the trade. I think before the French treaty is brought up for ratification the government ought to be able to give this House information with reference to this proposed revision, what is being done about it in the French Chambers. The other point is one I brought to the attention of the House in the budget debate. The United States tariff is not yet fixed. We do not exactly know what it will be, but there is not much doubt but that there will be some provisions in that tariff which will probably make us sit up and think with reference to our relations with other countries. That would be another consideration why it would not be well to make the contract for ten years. Whilst I am anxious to do what we reasonably can to promote the trade, we must yet have regard to our own interests. These two considerations would lead me to think that it would be wise for us to make but the simple yearly arrangement this year, and another year we will be able to see where we are.

The contract for the present will be only for one year. It expires on the 1st of May, and we have to make a new contract rip-ht away, because the season of navigation is about to open. I think the intention of my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is simply to make a contract for one year, until we have more definite information from France as to the application of the treaty.

The Allan contractors are entitled to the highest consideration, because not only were they the pioneers of the service between England and our own country, but in the beginning they laboured against great odds. Even during the period of this service with France they, have had a great many obstacles to contend with. Does my hon. friend mean that this contract is for one year only?
The contract made last year is only for one year, and it is the intention to renew it for one year only.

Am I mistaken in thinking that after the treaty has been accepted by

the French Chambers, it is still incomplete until it has been ratified by our own parliament?
Yes. The treaty which was made this year by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance will have to be submitted to parliament for its acceptance.
So it will be next session, before it is a finality?

No, I think my colleague the Minister of Finance is now in communication with the French government to find out when the treaty will be approved in France. We may prorogue very soon, and it is the intention of the government to bring down the treaty and ask parliament to approve of it.
The Minister of Finance stated, I think, the other day that we will not take it upon ourselves to ratify the treaty again until it has been finally approved by France.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Minister of Finance discussed this question with me a few days ago. It is not anticipated that there will be any difficulty on the part of France in accepting the treaty. The treaty was ratified last year, it has been modified since, but the modifications are not of such a nature as to make the treaty more difficult than it was from the French point of view. We have made it easier for France to ratify the treaty, therefore we do not apprehend that there will be any difficulty on the part of France. The French Chamber of Deputies has adjourned, but is going to resume early in May. The Minister of Finance I think is now in communication with the authorities in France, and I think it is his intention to submit the treaty to parliament this session for ratification.

When the treaty comes before us again we will have something to say about the marvellous achievements of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, for which he claimed great glory when he came home from France. I do not suppose there will be any expense this summer in connection with the ratification of that treaty, such as there was when my hon. friend returned from France on that occasion, and boasted that we were going to feed the whole of France with our fat cattle.
Is there a bonus given to the Hamburg-American line which runs between Canada and Hamburg, calling at an English port?
Not that I know of. There is a subsidy for a line to Antwerp.

I hope the minister, in making this contract, will arrange, if trade warrants it, to reach some port in the south of France as well as the port Mr. MONK
of Havre. Perhaps the minister will remember that when we were discussing the French treaty last year, I stated the view of some importers of French goods in Montreal that we lost the benefit of a considerable trade that might come to us', under the treaty, from the southern ports of France because of the fact that there is not a line of steamers between Canada and any of these southern ports. It was pointed out that, in the case of quite a number of exports from southern France, if they had to be sent by rail across France to Havre to take advantage of the direct steamship line the railways would be practically prohibitive of the exportation. May I ask the minister to endeavour, if he can, to make it possible later on, when the trade warrants it, for the government to secure a steamer service from the southern as well as from the northern ports.
As my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) is aware, most of the business done to-day is done with Le Havre. I admit that there are some exportations from the southern part of France.
From the port of Marseilles.

Yes, but the business to-day would not warrant us in making a contract for a direct line from Marseilles or any other southern port. If a line were established to southern France, of course it would be to the port of Marseilles, that being the most important. It may be, as my hon. friend suggests, that, at some time in the future, trade may warrant the establishment of a line between Canada and Marseilles, or having the present steamers call at Marseilles. At present, it is only contemplated to establish a line between Le Havre and Canada. Under this law, the suggestion of my hon. friend can be considered.

In connection with the trade of the Mediterranean, I recently received a letter from Syria, the scene of the massacres. It was written before the massacres began, and I do not know whether the gentleman who wrote to me has gone down or not. He pointed out that there was a great trade to be done between Canada and Syria. He went on to explain the difficulty they experience in obtaining the class of goods that Canada exports, and gave the prices at which these goods are sold there. He asks me to bring the letter to the attention of some commercial houses in Canada. If it will be to the advantage of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I shall be glad to hand it to either. I am sorrv I have not it here that I might read it to the committee. He writes from Beirut

and says that there is this large trade to be done with Canada if we had a steamship line with trips once a month or as often as the trade might warrant.
Can my hon. friend (Mr. Brodeur) tell me how he and his colleague came to forget, while negotiating in France, the existence of that Swiss treaty which was an obstacle to the final settlement?

Perhaps the fault does not lie entirely with us. I remember having read a question and answer given in the House in the year 1895, when the first French treaty was brought before the House. The government of that time was asked what were the nations enjoying most favoured nation treatment, and in the answer Switzerland was omitted. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs, later, published a book containing the names of the countries enjoying favoured nation treatment, and he followed the answer which had been given and omitted Switzerland. There has always been great doubt as to whether Switzerland occupied this position or not. Some legal gentlemen, with whom I had occasion, not very long ago, to discuss this question, were of opinion, after having read the provisions of the treaty of 1885 that this treaty did not apply to Canada so far as the favoured nation stipulation was considered. At one time there was doubt expressed also by the imperial government in the matter.

I think it is to be regretted that, when the hon. gentleman entered into negotiations, he and his colleague did not consider this. As a matter of fact, we have recognized since that, the Swiss treaty Bill.

Yes.

Bill (No. 152) to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act-Mr. Brodeur-read the second time and House went into committee thereon. |

Under the present law, when a wreck is a menace to navigation, we give notice to the vessel owner to remove the wreck. If he does not do it, we advertise in the papers asking for tenders for the removal. It happens very often that, in the meantime, the owners remove from the vessel everything that is worth .while, and when we come to remove the hull or to give a contract for its removal, we find that there is hardly anything of value. This means expenditure by the government. The object of this legislation is to declare that not only the vessel shall be a guar-165
antee of the cost of removal of the wreck, but also what is in the vessel, equipment, tackle and machinery.

Does that mean that if a vessel comes to grief with a valuable cargo on it, the owner of the vessel has to let the cargo go and await the long period which will elapse before the department gets its machinery in operation to remove the wreck?
No, we provide in subsequent sections that the wreck will have to be removed immediately, and if they do not remove it we will do it ourselves.

Immediate is a relative word. The cargo might be of a kind which, if it were necessary under the law to allow it to remain with the vessel, might be rendered of no use. Surely, if a man owns a vessel, if he has a cargo in it, if the vessel meets with a mishap and it goes down, he should have the opportunity of taking out such part of his cargo as is valuable as soon as possible and of saving it in the best condition. Is he absolutely prohibited from removing any part of the cargo?

No, in that case he
would have the right to give us a guarantee that the removal of the cargo would not be detrimental to the interests of the department.
Are there any cases that have given rise to this legislation?
Yes. In almost all of the cases that come before the department thev remove what is the most important and valuable part of the vessel leaving the hull which is generally not worth anything.
Will my hon. friend give an instance?

We had a case'in the west lately where a vessel sank. They removed the cargo and there was nothing of value left to us. We had to take the necessary proceedings to remove the wreck and it was done at a great cost to the department without anv revenue being derived from it. The country had to bear the expense. If the cargo had remained, or if it had been removed under a bond guaranteeing that this cargo would serve first for the payment of the cost of the removal of the wreck, there would have been something saved to the department.
What did it cost in that instance?

I have not the information now as to how much it cost. Tn some cases it costs us large sums of money. Last year we asked for public tenders for the removal of a wreck at the mouth of the Saguenay and it cost us $12,000 although we" did not get anything for it.
What ship was that?
The 'Protector.'

Suppose a vessel goes down in navigable waters, is the equipment of the vessel-her anchors, chains, &c.-to remain there until a bond is given? How long has it to remain or where has it to remain? The anchors, chains, &c., would have to be removed before the hull could be removed.

We expect in that case they will proceed right away to remove the wreck, but they will not be permitted to remove the equipment without giving a guarantee that this equipment will be considered as a part of the vessel. We will therefore have adieu not only upon the hull of the vessel but also on the equipment for the purpose of reimbursing the department for the expenditure we make in removing the wreck.
Suppose the owner is incompetent to give a bond?
Then we will proceed right away to remove the wreck, either doing it ourselves or calling for tenders.

As my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has pointed out, most of the equipment would be destroyed or rendered practically valueless in the time that it might remain in the water before the government might remove it.
Mr; BRODEUR. No, if we proceed immediately there is no danger that this equipment will be destroyed. The anchors, chains, &c., will still be of the same value.

These wrecks usually occur in places that are dangerous from the presence of rocks or rapids. A vessel might go down in a place where, if she were left for a few days, the whole thing would be cleaned out. What would become of the cargo and equipment then? Would it not be better to provide that the cargo and equipment could be removed under government supervision to some place of safety and stored there until the wreck was removed? Then, if it became necessary for the government to remove the wreck, they would have the goods and equipment of the vessel in store upon which they would have a lien to recoup them as far as they would go for the expense they might have incurred in removing the hull. The owner could always remove the goods and this would be preferable to requiring him to give a bond. He might not be in such circumstances that he would be able to give a bond.

In considering this provision we must keep in mind the definition of a vessel under chapter 115 of the statute. I will read the clause and my bon. friend Mr. BRODEtTR.
will understand the advisability of adopting the section that we have now submitted to the consideration of the committee. Section 13 reads :
In this Act unless the context otherwise requires, ' vessels ' includes every description of ship, boat or craft of ever kind whether impelled by steam or otherwise or whether used as sea-going vessels or on inland waters only.
That is all there is as to the definition of a vessel and the result is that later on when we proceed to the removal of a wreck we have no lien upon the most important part of the wreck, the equipment, the ballast, cargo and the machinery. Yes.

I admit that we have not formally provided for that in the Bill, and if the committee think it advisable we might put in such a provision or it might be made the subject of regulation.

Under the law the owners or the insurance company will put themselves in communication with the department at once. We want to have our lien on the material wherever it may be.
It might be done by having the material stored in the public warehouse.

of the wreck. Sometimes the government are very slow in acting whereas the owner of the cargo or vessel will be interested in proceeding at once with salvage operations. There may be doubt as to whether the government would remove the wreck.

BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 154) respecting the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal.

The port of Montreal is that part of the St. Lawrence river which extends from Portneuf to Montreal. My hon. friend remembers that some years ago that part of the St. Lawrence was under the control of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. Until 1888 all the work done between Quebec and Montreal was done by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal. In 1889 a change was made, and the government assumed the debt the Harbour Commissioners had incurred for

dredging that part of the St. Lawrence. The Harbour Commissioners, however, remained the pilotage authority for that part ' of the river until 1903, when an Act was passed providing that in future the pilotage authority should be vested in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, but there was no change made in the Harbour Commissioners Act itself. The statute I have just mentioned was a special one, declaring that the Department of Marine and Fisheries would henceforth be the pilotage authority, and control the pilots between Montreal and Quebec. Since that time the Harbour Commissioners have ceased to exercise any jurisdiction over the port of Montreal as a pilotage authority, but they have continued to exercise the right of making the rules of the road in that part of the St. Lawrence river. In the port of Quebec the rules of the road are prepared by this department, and in all the other navigable waters of the country as well. The only authority by which the Tules of the road, which had not been changed for many years, could be prepared or changed, was the Montreal Harbour Commissioners. Bill (No. 149) to amend the Extradition Act-Mr. Aylesworth-read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
*
Depositions for use in a foreign state may be taken in absence of accused.
I think we ought to have some explanation about this. It is interfering with the rights of the man accused.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: I admit that there seems to be a need of some remedy for the state of affairs mentioned by the minister, but I doubt very much whether we are giving the power to the right tribunal. We are giving to laymen, who have very little ability to protect the absent man, however good their intentions, power to deal with evidence to be used against that man in a foreign state, in extradition proceedings. While I would be in favour of some remedy for the condition described by the minister I would strongly urge that the taking of these depositions should not be entrusted to any one of a lower legal standing than a county court or district judge who would be able to rule out leading or improper questions, and to see that the interests of the absent man were protected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think on further consideration the hon. gentleman will agree that there is no danger in the Bill as drawn. These depositions as taken are not to be acted upon by the magistrate but are to be sent to the foreign country where the accused person is and will be passed on by the tribunal there. Before that tribunal objections may be urged on behalf of the accused to the regularity of the depositions, the authority under which they are taken, and the admissibility of evidence given. There may be applications for habeas corpus in the foreign state, after the accused person is committed for extradition, in that state by the proper official, who in the first instance would inquire into the sufficiency of these depositions, so the duty
which is imposed on the magistrate is simply the duty which all magistrates will discharge not only in the case of fugitives from foreign countries, but also in the case of Canadians who may be arrested on any criminal charge and brought before a magistrate for preliminary hearing. We have entrusted magistrates in such cases with the duty not only of taking the depositions, but also of passing upon them, committing a prisoner for trial. If we can safely entrust that duty to our magistrates in the ordinary case of a Canadian citizen accused in Canada of some criminal offence, why -may we not with equal safety entrust the like duty to a magistrate in the case of a fugitive from Canadian justice, especially when the magistrate does not pass upon the evidence he takes?

The answer to that is that in one case the man is present, it is all done before his face and the British principle that no man shall be proceeded against in his absence is not departed from, but here you are proceeding against a man in a foreign country in his absence. Then of course these depositions taken before the magistrate are not in the form of question and answer, they are converted by the magistrate into narrative form and every lawyer knows how frequently both counsel and accused, when a deposition is being read over before being signed, see that the magistrate's narrative report does not convey just what the man intended to say. Unless these depositions are taken before men of legal training and experience, such as the judges I have mentioned, you will certainly have many statements taken down and signed by witnesses that would not be signed in that form if the accused was present and understood how to protect himself or if he was represented by counsel who would see that the statements were correctly taken down and the cross-examination conducted.
I want to impress this upon the minister, and I think that he will find in the course of a year or two if not in the course of a day or two, that what I am saying is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that every piece of magisterial work could probably be better done by the county judge than by the average magistrate in the country. The county judge is, in virtue of his office, a magistrate for his county; but the difficulty is not only in increasing measurably the work of the county judge, but also in the circumstance that the countv judge is not within easy access of every man in his county. Not all the jurisdictions of county judges are as small as many Ontario counties with which we are familiar. Think of the tremendous distances in the least thickly settled portions of Canada, where men may be needed as witnesses upon a preliminary

inquiry of this sort who reside hundreds of miles from the county seat, where the county judge is to be found. I think these considerations will convince any one that it is better that work of this sort should be as far as possible decentralized. Then consideration should be given to the purpose for which these depositions are required, and for which alone they are to be used. They are not for the trial of the charge in any sense. I am not certain at the moment whether, in the absence of the witness, they could be used on a trial. The trial is to take place after the fugitive is brought into Canada, and the depositions only answer the purpose of securing his presence in Canada, from which perhaps in most cases he should never have departed. The depositions would no doubt be better taken in shorthand, in the form of question and answer; but that is not practicable. I am sure that my hon. friend can remember, as I can, when we had no shorthand reporters even in our high courts in Ontario at the trials of actions. We had to get along in the best way we could with evidence noted by a judge, which was often the only material on which an appeal in an important civil case could be taken. We have now the better system of taking the evidence in shorthand and extending it in full in question and answer, but that is not practicable in every minor proceeding, and this evidence being, only to secure the presence in Canada of the fugitive person, it seems to me that it is sufficient to leave it to a magistrate, even though taken down in ordinary longhand.

I am sorry that the hon. minister does not fall in with the view of the hon. member for Lincoln. I had not given much thought to the matter, but having listened to what he has said, I am very much impressed with the importance of having this evidence taken by a judge. We are taking a proceeding which is contrary to the ordinary common law practice in criminal matters when we provide that the evidence may be taken in the absence of the accused. But every person must see the necessity of it in this case, and I do not think that any one is disposed to question the wisdom of the Minister of Justice in making provision along these lines. I entirely commend the legislation that far. But the minister must not argue it on the basis of an every-day transaction. He has spoken as if it might occur several times a week and in several counties, but we must bear in mind that this extraordinary procedure is resorted to only in a case which involves and justifies a good deal of work. It is only in a case of a serious crime, and it is a serious matter for a man to be removed from a place which he has chosen as his domicile, unless there is a clear strong prima facie case made out against Mr. AYLESWORTH.
him, and that should be made out on legitimate evidence reasonably obtained. We do not think that we are surrounding a case with any more than reasonable safeguards when we say that this evidence should be taken before some one capable of judging the bearing of evidence and the proper manner of adducing it. It is not enough to say that this evidence, when it comes before the foreign tribunal, may be objected to by counsel on behalf of the accused. It may not be objected to, because the accused may have no counsel to raise an objection on his behalf. But even if he has a counsel, and if his counsel is ever so astute, the evidence presents a certain aspect, when it is produced before that foreign tribunal, which is governed, not by the importance of the facts, but by the manner in which the evidence has been taken. The result is that to the foreign tribunal it presents a picture altogether contrary to the true facts of the case. Perhaps no one has been there to guard the interests of the accused; perhaps the evidence has been elicited by a detective, who is interested to an enormous extent in running down the accused and bringing him back to Canada. All lawyers know the length to which men of that class will go and the methods by which they work. Get a magistrate who is without experience in the law taking down evidence at the dictation of a constable or a detective in the absence of the accused, and you are doing something that is very dangerous. I think that the very least safeguard we should insist upon in these cases is that the evidence should be taken before a judge of a county court or of a district court or before a judge of the high court. The minister has said that one reason against it is the throwing of too heavy a burden upon the county judges. That is not a well-taken argument. If there is anything we want in this country, it is in many instances that the county judges may have more work to keep them occupied; because, as an hon. friend says, they are rusting out rather than wearing out. In some counties it is necessary to have two judges, because one is sometimes absent holding division courts, though there is perhaps not enough work for one. In other cases there is only work for a judge and a half, and you must have the two. We are not throwing too great a burden on the county judges when we ask them to do this work and we are giving them work which many of them will be quite ready to do because it is in the interests of honest and effective administration of justice. In how many cases in any county in a whole year would you throw this duty on a county judge? In not one in a county in a year. In not one, as a rule, in a score of years, so that the argument that this would throw too heavy a burden on the county court

judges is not entitled to any weight. Surely the hon. minister was not taking a photograph of the real situation when he talked of the accused having to travel probably a hundred miles in order to give his testimony before a judge. I venture to say it would be very rare indeed when he would have to travel even 25 miles, and the probability would be very remote of his ever having to travel one hundred miles. But even if he had, that would be ten thousand times better than that we should set aside any of the necessary safeguards in the interests of the person accused. The suggestion of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) is a very judicious one.

My hon. friend is talking entirely from the standpoint of the province of Ontario, where they have a county court judge and in some cases two for each county. But it may surprise him to learn that down in the maritime provinces we have often but one county court judge for four or five counties. In my portion of the province of New Brunswick, the district administered by the county court judge is over 200 miles in length, and on the north shore of New Brunswick there are four counties with but one county court judge. The amendment is hardly fair to the intelligence of the average magistrate in Canada. As far as my experience goes, a magistrate can take down evidence and draw conclusions fairly well. If a magistrate is given authority to take the depositions of the accused in so important a matter as a murder, I do not see why he cannot take depositions which may be acted on in a foreign country for the purpose of obtaining witnesses. My hon. friends are drawing on their imaginations for difficulties which do not exist. If this Bill passes, no harm could be done, and in many parts of Canada great difficulties will be caused if we oblige a county court judge to travel 100 or 200 miles to take depositions.

I was not speaking of the average intelligence of the magistrate of Ontario or any other province, but of the fact that in some isolated cases the magistrates are not very intelligent men. These may be only isolated cases, and I would not be surprised if some were _ in my hon. friend's province as well as mine; and the average intelligence in Ontario will compare fairly with that in any other province. What applies to the general public would apply to the( magistrate as well. Our magistrates have been selected from good motives in many cases, and as a rule are an excellent class of men, but there are instances where they do not possess any great degree of education and have no judicial training. Therefore I
think that the Minister of Justice would be wise in not having legislation enacted in this form.

I want to add my approval to what has been said by hon. members on this side. Is the Minister of Justice aware that there are provisions in the statute now, under which depositions taken by a magistrate may be read against the accused on his trial under certain circumstances and as this law stands, such depositions are taken in his absence. If this Bill should pass, I take it that the general provisions of the Code will apply, and we will have evidence taken against the accused in his absence read against him in his trial when he comes back to this country, and upon such evidence he might possibly be convicted. If the minister thinks it necessary, as I believe it is, to have some such provision made as is made in this Bill, then the interests of the accused should be safeguarded to the extent of providing that such evidence taken in his absence should not be used against him on his trial, if there is any doubt whatever about the right to have it read.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not prepared to express any opinion whether, on the death of a witness, a deposition taken for the purpose of extradition could be read at the trial. I should doubt it. It may be so according to the language of the provision of the Act which permits depositions to be read in such cases as I have described, but I would not accept that view without much more careful consideration and examination of the statute than I have been able to give it. But the whole question is surely whether or not the existing state of things is preferable to that which would arise should this Bill become law. Under the existing conditions, these depositions are in practice taken before a magistrate in the absence of the accused. They are taken, it may be, without sufficient legal warrant. I do not know that that question has ever been raised in a foreign state, but it is liable to be Taised, and it is to meet such an objection, if it should be raised, that this Bill is designed. At the present time, there is nothing to prevent the magistrate, when the information is laid before him upon which it is desired to get proceedings instituted for extradition, withholding his action until he shall have taken, as a part of the material on which he shall issue his warrant, all the depositions that any witness who may choose to appear before him may make. That is done in practice in, I suppose, all or nearly all, of the cases of accusations for extradition. I am not prepared to say that that is an irregular practice, but it is one for which there is no express statutory war-

rant. The whole effect of this Bill will be that the magistrate before whom the information is laid, the magistrate who receives the charge may, after having so received it summon witnesses and take their depositions.
Does the minister think that that is evidence that should be read against a man on his trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Porter) wants an answer categorically whether I think that ought to be read. I am free to say that I see no more danger in doing it in the case of a person charged for extradition than in doing it in the case of a person who is in this country and who may have been present and may have been objecting as much as he pleases. He is subject to the same magistrate's rulings which, upon the hypothesis of hon. gentlemen who have spoken, are going to be without authority and without judicial character. He is subject to the same illiterate magistrate-if there be one-in taking down the evidence incorrectly. That if it is the present condition of things, arises from the circumstance of men being selected as magistrates who are not properly fitted for that position.

When the minister cannot see any difference in the protection afforded to a prisoner between having evidence given when he is present and having it given when he is absent, it is hopeless to argue with him. Under the circumstances, i have two things to say about the matter, the first ia that the Bill should not be gone on with, and the second is that it is useless to argue with the minister on the merits of the question.
In view of what the minister said, why not provide in this Bill that such evidence when taken should not be read against the prisoner at his trial? Make it certain.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Porter) say that in this Bill there ought to be a clause stating that such deposition should not be read at the trial of the accused?
Yes, make it certain.
Suppose the witness is dead?

All the more reason why the evidence should not be read, for you would be using evidence concerning which you cannot punish the person if perjury has been committed. Is there no idea in the head of the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau) or of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) that a man accused has some rights in this country? Have they no idea that harm may be done by taking evidence behind his back before a magistrate who, instead of having the evidence reported in Mr. AYLESWORTH.
the form of question and answer, transposes it into narrative form? As has been well said by the hon. member for West Hastings, the detective or person interested in getting a conviction goes before the magistrate, and it is all one-sided, the accused not being present or represented. And what the detective or magistrate may be tricky or ignorant enough to do, the Minister of Justice, apparently, is approving by his legislation. There is nobody there on behalf of the prisoner-nobody can be there, for they do not know what is being done. They have no knowledge that the poll is to be held, so to sneak, at that time, and they have no idea that they are being dealt with on that occasion. And the evidence, instead of being taken down in auestion and answer form, the only way in which one can readily judge of what the witness said, is transposed by these people into narrative form behind the back of the accused. And this evidence so taken is to be used against him. The Solicitor General says: 'Suppose the witness is dead.' The witness is the onlv person, it may be, beside the magistrate, who knows anything about it, the prisoner not being there and not being represented. The very fact that the witness is dead is all the greater reason why the evidence should not be read, because the witness cannot be proceeded against for perjury or asked to explain it.
How about the other witnesses, if perjury can be proved?

Who is going to bring these other witnesses? And how are you going to convict when you do not know what is going on? You are taking away a man's liberty or taking a step towards it, and that may mean the same thing in the end. The Solicitor General said:	'How
about the other witnesses?' Who knows about the other witnesses? How does the accused know of the evidence that is being given affecting his liberty and that may lead to his being taken from a foreign country where he has his domicile? He may be completely innocent. Suppose he is charged with forgery, a witness testifies against him, though he knows nothing of the proceedings. The witness simply says: 'That is not my signature on that bill; or, That is not my father's signature.' The magistrate transposes that in such a way that, on the face of it, the witness has sworn that the accused forged that bill. There is no opportunity for cross examination, no opportunity for the accused to show that, for instance, he had the authority of the man to sign the bill in his name. My hon. friend speaks of a case of murder tried in the presence of the accused. If the accused is present, he is to be blamed if he does not see to it that things are done cor-

rectly, or employ a counsel who will protect his interests. His friends may inter- ' pose if he is too weak-minded to attend to his own defence. Or some charitably disposed man may interfere to see that the prisoner gets justice. Or, as is well said by ' a friend near me, the court may say as it often says in such cases: 'This is a serious accusation and this prisoner should be defended,' and may pick upon some counsel and ask him, in the interest of justice to see to it that the accused gets a fair trial. So much is this a recognized practice that it is considered, if not exactly contempt of court, an impolite thing for counsel not to accept the appointment and see that the man gets a fair trial. But here is the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth), with the Solicitor-General (Mr. Bureau) apparently agreeing with him, saying that it is no harm to take all these proceedings behind a man's back, with no one there to represent him to see that the evidence is taken down by a judicially-minded officer, no opportunity for him to engage counsel to see to it that the evidence is taken down in the shape that would be directed by a judge who knows what evidence is.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) wants to be fair about this.
I am satisfied that he is not trying unduly to prevent the passage of this Bill. But I think he has failed to appreciate the real meaning and intention of the Bill. My hon. friend is discussing what may happen at the trial in case of the death or absence of a witness. I have not examined the Code, but I am satisfied that the only evidence which can be read at the trial is the evidence given at the preliminary examination by a witness who is either dead or absent from the country.

The Minister of Justice
won't take that responsibility.

This does not refer to the preliminary examination at all, but to the evidence being given by a witness to be used in the foreign country for the arrest of the supposed criminal for the purpose of bringing him to this country to take his trial, and when he is brought here on this evidence, then he must have his preliminary examination.
No, he goes right to the extradition commission.
No, he must have his preliminary examination.
Before whom does he have his present examination?
He goes to the person who issues the order for his arrest.
He goes to the county court judge directly.

No, I am satisfied I am correct. Therefore I contend my hon. friend is making a mountain out of a mole hill, he is conjuring up something in his mind that does not exist. He raised the question first whether this evidence should be taken before a justice of the peace or a county court judge. I cannot see why a justice of the peace cannot take down evidence just as intelligently as a county court judge. If the evidence is admitted, due respect would be given to that fact before the foreign tribunal.
If the Minister of Justice will confirm what has just been said by my hon. friend from Carleton, that that evidence cannot be read against him at his trial, I will withdraw my objection.

I cannot answer for the Minister of Justice, but my hon. friend can see by the Bill itself that the only object of getting the evidence is to send it to the foreign country. I submit that the only deposition which can be read at the trial of an accused person is the deposition taken at the preliminary examination. But this is not a preliminary examination, this is only an examination for the purpose of getting evidence to be sent to the foreign country.

The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) may be satisfied, but we have the statement of the Minister of Justice that he is not sure, he will take chances with it and let it go whichever way it may. But the Solicitor General says that if the witness is dead, why, so much the better, it is all right. I am prepared to say that we are encountering a great danger. My hon. friend from Lincoln and Niagara took the case of forgery. A man who gives evidence in the absence of the accused may be the man whose monetary interest is at stake, he may be the man who is shielding himself by accusing another, who is saving his pocket by accusing another. But the Minister of Justice is prepared to take chances of that form of evidence upon which this man may be ultimately tried and convicted.

There is no doubt that the deposition cannot be used. This section merely provides that the evidence may be taken as if such accused person was present and charged with such extradition crime. Section 999 provides:	[DOT]
If upon the trial of an accused person such facts are proved upon oath or affirmation that it can be reasonably inferred therefrom that any person whose evidence was given at any former trial upon the same charge or whose deposition has been therefore taken in the investigation of the charge against such accused person, is dead, or is so ill as not to be able to travel, or is absent from Canada, and if it is proved that such evidence was

given or that such deposition was taken in the presence of the person accused
Does the hon. gentleman say that those words do not cover this evidence?
No doubt they do not cover it.
I think that ought to satisfy the hon. member for Simcoe.

It provides that the evidence shall be taken as if the person accused were present, it does not provide that it shall be subsequently used as if the person were present. Unless there is such a provision as that the condition required to be complied with by section 999 would prevent the introduction of such evidence. The requirement is that the evidence shall be taken in the presence of the person accused, and that he or his counsel shall have full opportunity of examining the witness. This Bill says it shall be taken as though he were present, it is to be taken as if he were present for the purpose of being sent to the United States or other foreign country to support the extradition warrant there. The same principle prevails here as in the United States, and merely validates the existing practice in this country. With regard to taking evidence before a county court or superior court judge, the greatest objection is that this evidence as a rule requires to be taken with dispatch in order that it may reach the place in which it is to be used and secure the extradition of the criminal. It is necessary that it should be promptly taken, and you cannot get it promptly taken in many places in Canada if you require it to be taken before a county court or a superior court judge. Such requirement may necessitate the judge or the witness travelling a great distance. This evidence is worthless in 99 cases out of 100 unless it is taken with a promptitude that is not usually possible if it must be taken before a county court or a superior court judge. In my experience I think the majority of magistrates take evidence of this kind quite as well as the judges. I do not know where evidence is more carefully taken than it is generally taken by magistrates.
Bill reported.

I would call my right hon. friend's attention to the fact that we are Mr. CONGDON.
nearing the end of the session, and it i3 essential that we should know, in order to exDedite and facilitate the business, exactly what is going to be taken up on the following day. To-morrow many of us will be absent. Are we going to take up Bills, as my hon. friend has said, indiscriminately? Shall we take the Rill on immigration? We are all anxious to advance the business of the House and it would aid us in doing that if we could know almost exactly what is going to be the business of the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I said to my hon. friend that our intention was to take up Bills, commencing with the Grand Trunk Bill. We intend to follow the order on the paper and to take the Immigration Bill to suit the convenience of my hon. friends. If they are not prepared to go on with the Immigration Bill we will not take it up.
My right hon. friend knows that if we take up the Grand Trunk Bill it will probably obviate the necessity of taking up the Immigration Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I hope not. I hope we can take the Grand Trunk and other Bills as well.
Is there a probability that the Grand Trunk Bill will be taken up?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I say it will be taken up first.
